1ddf5d5b1ba7f547: Well, it’s official: Anthropic will become the first publicly-traded frontier AI lab in history come the opening of markets on Thursday.

The company's most recent SEC filing cites that price range but allows for the possibility of a higher price, which should be determined Wednesday night.
Late on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported that Anthropic would price at $83, citing people familiar. Whatever the case, Anthropic is likely to be valued at more than $1 trillion.

Anthropic’s debutante ball has been on the horizon for a while, and documents leaked in late September made it all the more inevitable as the company’s finances revved up and it sought to capture the momentum of its best quarter to date before things start to tail off.

The company revised its IPO documents on November 2, warning that the 12x growth it was touting was unlikely to continue in the long term due to compute infrastructure investments to the tune of nearly $900 billion it was on the hook for over the next few years.

"In the nine months ended September 30, 2026, our revenue was $33.2 billion, representing a year-over-year growth rate of 1,206%," the revised prospectus reads. "We do not expect our revenue will continue to grow at comparable rates, and we cannot assure you that it will continue to grow at all."

It’s possible, in other words, that Anthropic may never be a money maker despite the hype and its position as the first mover. The IPO prospectus is short on answers to critical questions and leaves a lot unanswered - like, for example, whether it’s going to actually be able to pay its bills.

"Our ability to meet the substantial and growing financial obligations of these requirements to secure compute depends on our ability to generate significant revenue growth," the updated prospectus admits.
Investors don’t seem to care right now, though.
Anthropic already has compute commitments amounting to roughly $70.7 billion in the next 12 months. That’s just shy of its $81 billion run-rate as of October 31.
Expect more hot air to be injected tomorrow, adding additional surface tension and the possibility of even more losses if, and when, this monster pops. ®

6c55e765797bce3c: SEOUL: Governments around the world sounded the alarm on Wednesday over a critical flaw in the popular programming language Java that could allow hackers to access computer systems, the latest high-profile cyber incident in recent weeks.
US tech firm Calif, which last month found a cybersecurity flaw in another programming language, PHP, said it had discovered a bug in Java's memory functions.
The vulnerability could allow hackers to remotely execute code or to crash systems.

US, South Korean, German and British authorities and China's Tencent urged companies and organisations to install a fix for the vulnerability, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency said it was investigating the issue.

Concern was particularly acute in South Korea, where Java is heavily used. The presidential office held an emergency meeting on Tuesday with government agencies to discuss preemptive measures to tackle the threat, the Yonhap news agency reported.
Java widely used globally by public and private sectors

Java, available from Oracle as well as from open-source Java development kits, is one of the world's most widely used programming languages and is used in critical information systems spanning government agencies, the corporate sector and financial institutions as well as the military.
Recent technology outages and heightened concerns over software vulnerabilities have put a fresh spotlight on corporate cybersecurity and the resilience of critical IT infrastructure.
Shares in cybersecurity providers CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks were up more than 5.6%, among the biggest gainers on the S&P 500, in late morning trading in New York.
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency said in an advisory that the vulnerability required immediate patching. It did not link it to any recent outages.

Tencent Cloud, the cloud-computing arm of Chinese technology company Tencent, warned customers on Wednesday that the vulnerability in the open-source kit, known as "Java4Shell", could allow unauthenticated attackers to steal sensitive information or take control of affected servers.

German and Dutch cybersecurity agencies said there were currently no known successful attacks exploiting the vulnerability. Britain's cybersecurity agency urged companies and organisations to keep systems up to date "during this unprecedented time".
Oracle could not be immediately reached for comment, but it issued a software update for its Java Development Kit on Nov 17 that contains fixes for the flaw.

The warnings come amid several major technology disruptions including one at the US National Security Agency on Tuesday, although authorities and companies have not linked them to the Java vulnerability.
Apple also suffered an outage on Tuesday after an internal update that affected customer services including iCloud and Apple Pay. Systems were restored on Wednesday.
AI makes it easier for hackers

Cybersecurity concerns have intensified this year as rapid advances in artificial intelligence give both attackers and defenders increasingly powerful tools, while a series of technology outages in recent days has underscored the fragility of critical systems.

AI can make it faster and easier for hackers to identify and exploit weaknesses, shrinking the window for companies to patch vulnerabilities from what could once have been days to potentially hours or minutes.

Last month, governments and companies around the world took websites offline as a precaution while website operators scrambled to secure systems running PHP software after Calif disclosed the vulnerability.
Cybersecurity companies regularly uncover examples of hackers using AI to launch scores of intrusions at once.

Companies are also deploying AI to scan their own systems for vulnerabilities and are rushing to fix what they find, a process that carries risks of its own, Surfshark's lead system engineer Karolis Kaciulis said.
"Patching that much, that quickly, makes systems less stable," he said.

The spate of tech outages over the past week has ranged from disruptions to many Microsoft services including email, to a halt to US air travel that lasted 4-1/2 hours and a JPMorgan Chase software problem that interfered with some banking services.

US president Donald Trump's administration has played down concerns about a broader problem, with secretary of state Marco Rubio, who doubles as national security adviser, acknowledging that the incidents were "unsettling" but adding that they were completely unrelated.
South Korea vulnerable as heavy Java user
China and South Korea are among countries with significant Java developer communities, according to surveys by software development tools maker JetBrains.

A 2025 JetBrains survey found that 37% of respondents to its Java-focused study were based in mainland China. That reflects the survey sample rather than the countries' shares of the global Java developer population.
Java represented 53% of programming language use in South Korea compared with a global average of 30%, a 2021 JetBrains survey said.
Its use was even higher in South Korea's public sector, accounting for a 72% share of programming language use for information systems, according to a South Korean government survey last year.

535ee02d0cd9e1ad: Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.

These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.

As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.
Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently.
Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.”

“We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.”

NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version.
On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible.

Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.
All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5.

“Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld said in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.”

Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8.

Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.”

The AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers.
AI-powered bug hunting for the win?

"While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company said in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance."

All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation .

“AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.”
There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.”

But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities.
“Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz said.®

e7b812635d3e1aa9: WASHINGTON: Hakeem Jeffries vowed Wednesday to "hold the crooks accountable" after Democrats nominated him to become the first Black speaker of the US House of Representatives, setting the stage for two years of confrontation with President Donald Trump.

The 56-year-old New Yorker is poised to preside over a commanding Democratic majority following his party's sweeping midterm election victory, as his lawmakers prepare to reverse Republican policies and investigate the Trump administration.

Jeffries faced no declared challenger in the closed-door party election, but resistance from some newly elected progressives highlighted divisions over how Democrats should wield their newfound power.

"We're going to fight to make sure that, in the face of the unprecedented corruption, chaos, and cruelty visited upon the American people, that House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones, because the American people deserve better," Jeffries told reporters.
His warning came as Democrats unveiled plans for wide-ranging investigations into Trump officials and his business interests when they take control of the House in January.

Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, sent 12 letters Wednesday warning members of Trump's family and senior administration figures to preserve documents ahead of investigations into alleged corruption, immigration abuses and the handling of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
"This is just the beginning," Garcia said.
Historic milestone
Jeffries secured 251 votes in a secret ballot, with 11 cast against his nomination, according to US media.
He must still win a formal vote of the full House when the new Congress convenes on Jan 3, but the election is expected to be a formality given the Democrats' commanding majority.
He would become the first Black politician to occupy the powerful position, presiding over the House during the final two years of Trump's presidency.

Both returning Democrats and incoming lawmakers participated in Wednesday's ballot, with some progressives seeking concessions on issues ranging from US military support for Israel to the influence of money in politics.
Individual votes remained secret, with only the overall tally made public.

Ahead of the election, Jeffries met progressive lawmakers to discuss issues including Israel and healthcare, and he pledged Wednesday to tackle the cost-of-living crisis that helped propel Democrats to victory.
Brooklyn roots

"Our message to the American people, who are struggling in this failed economy, is a simple one: we hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you," he said.
"We're going to fight for an affordable America."
Raised in Brooklyn's working-class Crown Heights neighborhood, Jeffries trained as a lawyer before entering the New York state legislature in 2007 and winning election to Congress in 2012.

Known for his measured manner, sharp rhetoric and penchant for quoting hip-hop artists, he became the first Black politician to lead a party in either chamber of Congress when Democrats chose him to succeed Nancy Pelosi in 2022.
He also served as a House prosecutor during Trump's first impeachment trial in 2020.
As speaker, Jeffries would preside over one of Washington's most powerful institutions and stand second in line to the presidency behind the vice president.
But he would face formidable challenges in managing a coalition spanning centrists and an increasingly assertive left flank, while pursuing legislation against a president who retains veto power.

748dee8b2bb6cd80: For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.

With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world.
Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today.
“These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week.
It’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with. And some believe it may be time for a rethink.
“What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier said.
For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity.
What happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he said. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.”
By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster.
“Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained.
This is problematic for the large clusters major hyperscalers and cloud providers are now building to fuel the AI boom. “All those systems are capacity systems,” Strohmaier said.

They’re not designed to run one piece of code but have instead been architected to run many, many smaller or medium-sized code instantiations, which may include training, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and of course inference.
Because of this, Strohmaier says, it wouldn’t be reasonable to expect SpaceXAI to run something High-Performance Linpack (HPL) on a cluster like Colossus.

But these clusters are still worth tracking. They'll just need a new benchmark better suited to judging the capability of these arrays while at the same time preventing operators from gaming the system.

What shape or form such a benchmark might take remains to be seen. Developing a new benchmark or methodology is no small task, and changing the existing benchmarks isn’t ideal. ”If we do anything to the benchmark itself, we’re going to lose the historic trends, which is extremely valuable,” Hoefler said.

Allowing for lower precisions — HPL-MxP already does this to some extent — is one avenue for addressing the fact that these accelerators are increasingly trading FP64 performance for lower-accuracy floating-point data types like FP8 or FP4.

Another avenue is developing a separate AI benchmark. This would be immediately applicable to these clusters, but with the pace of change in model architecture, building such a benchmark is challenging.
“The AI workloads change every two weeks, so if you pick something today, it’s going to be irrelevant in at most a year, and these benchmarks need to live for multiple decades,” Hoefler said. ®

ea2a682fdbb547e1: At The Money: Shopping Under Surveillance (November 18, 2026)

Ever feel like your most-used apps and favorite companies are playing games with you? Price changes from airlines, delivery services, and even Amazon seem to be all over the map. What does this mean for your wallet? L
Full transcript below.
About this week’s guest:
Lindsay Owens is CEO of the Groundwork Collaborative, a DC-based economic think tank and author of a new bestseller, “Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—and What That Means for Your Wallet.”
For more info, see:
Professional website
LinkedIn

Find all of the previous At the Money episodes here, and in the MiB feed on Apple Podcasts, YouTube, Spotify, and Bloomberg. And find the entire musical playlist of all the songs I have used on At the Money on Spotify
Transcript: Lindsay Owens, CEO of Groundwork Collaborative

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Ever feel like your most used apps and companies are playing games with you? Price changes from airlines, delivery services, even Amazon seem to be all over the map. What does this mean for your wallet?

To help us unpack all of this, let’s bring in Lindsay Owens. She’s CEO of Groundwork Collaborative. She’s also the author of a new book, Gouged: The End of a Fair Price and What That Means for Your Wallet. So let’s start out with some of the basics of surveillance capitalism and surveillance pricing that you describe in the book. Essentially, algorithms collecting all this data to try and guess what your willingness to pay might be.
Are we basically in a place where a price on the shelf for everybody, is that just a historical relic?

LINDSAY OWENS: Look, we’ve had price tags for almost 150 years now in this country. You know, for thousands of years we haggled. You went to the market, you picked out what you wanted, and then a negotiation commenced. But in the late 1800s, the Quakers felt like that wasn’t quite right. They thought haggling was unfair, all men should be treated equal, and they dispensed with the kind of greedy way that the Puritans were haggling, and they decided to use a fixed price.

And shortly after that, it was John Wanamaker, the iconic Philadelphia retailer, in his Wanamaker’s department store. He put the price tag on items for the first time, and we’ve been living under that kind of cultural and economic regime for nearly 150 years. But these days, I think the transparency and the predictability that a price tag provided is really under attack and at risk of extinction. Prices are changing, prices are more volatile, thanks to electronic shelf labels and algorithmic pricing. Prices are more deceptive. Sometimes you and I are charged different amounts for the same item thanks to personalized pricing or surveillance pricing.
So it really is a new frontier of pricing, and I would argue a new frontier of corporate profiteering.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. So let’s talk about some of the things that consumers can do, especially when it comes to online shopping or app shopping. What can we do to enhance our own digital privacy? How can we prevent stores from cranking up prices on us because of either where we live or our shopping history or any other information they know about us from online?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah. So the first thing I’ll say is, you know, I really don’t believe that it should be all of our jobs to duck and dodge and bob and weave and figure out how to beat the machine. I think we need fair and honest markets and fair and honest prices, and I think it’s the job of lawmakers to ensure that. But I also used to be a Hill staffer, so I know waiting around for Congress is not always your best bet.

So there are some things you can do. The first thing I like to say is they learn how much they can overcharge you by running experiments on you. Turn the experiment back around on them. You know, if you’re gonna buy your Christmas airplane tickets this year to go home and see Mom, sit down with your husband or your spouse and, you know, both of you fire up your computers at the same time and see if one of you gets a better deal on the tickets. There’s a good chance the ticket prices will be different for each of you. Go with whoever gets the cheapest price.

If you’re leaving a football game this weekend with a few friends and you’re gonna take an Uber home because you’ve had a couple beers, everyone fire up the Uber app at the same time, and probably one of you will get charged a lower price for the same ride to the same destination. Go with whoever gets the lower price. There is, I think, a simplicity in turning their experiments back around on them.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: A lot of us use loyalty programs. How do companies use the data for these programs where we think we’re getting a deal? How is that used against us?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, this is one of the saddest parts of the book, which is the revelation that you might be at risk of a loyalty penalty for using loyalty programs, right? You get really excited when you join a loyalty program in the beginning, ’cause you get promised all these perks and freebies and these inducements that get you to kind of hand over your data and shop attached to your loyalty card. But what we have started to see is the problem of the loyalty penalty. Once a company knows what you purchase on a regular basis, they figure that you’re a sure thing and they no longer need to push you any of those offers or discounts.

And there’s an example in the book from a Washington Post reporter who lived in a state that allowed him to request his data from Starbucks, and he got the 55-page report. And he learned that over time, as Starbucks knew he was a sure thing, he didn’t get any perks or freebies or discounts anymore. There was also a reporter recently from Wired magazine who requested his McDonald’s app data, by the way, so that was like a 500-page dossier.

I got to talk to him and I was like, I’m so excited to meet the Hamburglar. Like, you are really a serious customer. But one of the interesting things in his reporting was that McDonald’s had calculated this lifetime attrition score. Like, how likely is he to, like, you know, leave McDonald’s and go shop somewhere else, like Burger King? And his attrition score was zero.

They were like, he is absolutely hooked on McDonald’s. But these companies do use the data that they collect about you in loyalty programs, and they are pretty sophisticated data-harvesting operations in pricing and promotion decisions. And you can end up being penalized once they’ve got a full sense of your likely purchase history. The other thing they do, of course, which you may or may not care about, is they often bundle up your data and sell it, increasingly.

Companies like Kroger, you know, where 95% of transactions are attached to loyalty programs, they have an alternative profits book of business that is 30% of their net operating income. And a big piece of that is the sale of your data. So loyalty programs are a bit of a double-edged sword, I’d say.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. Tell us about dark patterns and drip pricing. Are companies really doing last-minute fees tacked on when you’re about to engage in a transaction?

LINDSAY OWENS: Oh yes. So drip pricing is the worst. It’s this practice of sort of luring you in with a teaser rate or a low initial price only to tack on, throughout the remainder of the transaction, drip, drip, drip, other fees, such that the total price you pay at the end is much higher than the teaser rate.

This is also, in some settings, called unbundling. Something that you’ve certainly experienced in the airlines, where, you know, the fare no longer includes things like your luggage or picking a seat, right? You have to pay extra for that. So, you know, drip pricing and junk fees are really tough, and they’re made much easier to use to exploit you in e-commerce because of things like dark patterns, the ways in which companies can manipulate user interfaces and make design choices that make it hard for you to see, you know, that these fees have been tacked on throughout the transaction.

We do, thanks to the Federal Trade Commission rulemaking that happened at the end of the Biden administration, now prohibit drip pricing in two sectors of the economy. So instead, you have to see the full and total price upfront. The first sector is short-term lodging. So if you’ve picked up an Airbnb or a Vrbo recently, you probably noticed that you can now see the full price of a week’s stay, inclusive of things like cleaning fees and stuff like that that used to be tacked on at the end.

And we also now require upfront pricing, or all-in pricing, in event ticketing. So you can see, you know, when you hover over a seat to pick a concert seat, you now see the full price of the ticket, not just the price of the seat. So it includes the price of the fees, and, you know, it doesn’t make the price any cheaper, but it does allow you to do a better job of comparison shopping, and it makes it such that you at least know the full price that you’re paying upfront before you start the transaction.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: What about subscription traps and roach motels? I have a handful of subscriptions and every now and then I try and cancel ’em and I get nowhere. Fortunately, I have a good relationship with my bank. We use the same corporate and personal bank, and when I say, “Hey, this is a fraud, they won’t let me cancel, stop paying this.” They’ve been pretty good about that, but I don’t think everybody has the same access to their private banker. What can you do about subscription traps and getting outta the roach motels?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, this is a tough one. A couple times in my life I’ve really been buried under subscriptions. Once when I was in high school, and I got pretty deep with the Columbia House records subscription programs,
BARRY RITHOLTZ: Everybody. Right? Hilarious.
LINDSAY OWENS: Oh man. It was just like, you know, you’re in
BARRY RITHOLTZ: High school. If you were in high school, you were a minor, you didn’t have contractual ability, and you could just send them a nasty letter.

LINDSAY OWENS: And that’s what I did. That’s in law school, I dealt with my Columbia Record House debt. I’m like, “Sorry, didn’t have contractual capacity as a 14-year-old. Bye-bye.” So eventually, but, you know, most times you don’t get that.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: And they were actually pretty good about canceling. You just had to remember to send the card in on time, and nobody did.

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah. The tough thing about the Columbia House was the negative option billing. So you picked out two discs at full price and then you got 12 discs for a penny. But then they would send you some discs that you didn’t select, and if you forgot to send them back, you had to pay full price for those too. So you could really end up kind of snowed under a pile of CDs. The other time in my life where I really got into trouble on subscriptions was right after I had my baby, and, you know, you’re not sleeping, you’ve got a lot going on.

And I ended up in a subscription for, like, a developmentally appropriate toy service. And actually it was a gift from a friend. She gave me three toy boxes, and at some point, like a year into my son’s life, I was like, why am I still getting these toy boxes? And I realized my friend had gifted me three months, but they had started charging me for them.
Right. So I think, you know, even though you never signed anything, you never agreed to anything. No, no. Oh, it was unbelievable.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: That’s an easy letter, CC’d to the state attorney general, and that’s the end of that. But still, I mean, good luck. What about the fact that these companies no longer have customer service branches? If you want to cancel satellite or cable, if you want to change something on your phone, it’s an hour of your life. It’s pretty horrendous.

LINDSAY OWENS: Yes. My organization has released model legislation that we call the Shopper’s Bill of Rights, and it includes 12 rights that we think shoppers should be guaranteed in the e-commerce and agent commerce era. And two of them include the right to a refund on the same payment method that you initially purchased it on, without battling a chatbot for three hours, and the right to cancellation the same way you signed up. If they auto-populated your address and your credit card information on the way in with one click, you can get out of that subscription with one click.

And New York City, actually, just about a week ago, implemented a click-to-cancel rule in the city. So companies operating in New York City have to give folks the same method of cancellation that they get for signing up for a subscription.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Let’s talk about something that’s kind of fascinating to me: the right to repair. So what started happening with everything from computers and printers to farm equipment, the company said, “You can’t fix this, you have to bring it back to us, and we’re gonna charge you an arm and a leg to do basic repairs,” or even things like buying cheaper toner for your printer. What about the right to repair and the right to shop for the components of that product?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, I think a lot of people are surprised to see this included in my book because they don’t always think of that kind of thing when they think of price gouging. But I absolutely think restraint of repair is a form of price gouging, and arguably a real daisy chain of price gouging, because they can, you know, charge you an arm and a leg for the initial product, then they charge you again for proprietary parts, then they might charge you again for proprietary labor, where, you know, you can’t fix it yourself, and maybe if you can’t fix it at all, you have to buy it again. So increasingly, companies use technology to make it hard to repair items. Car companies, you know, with engine control units that make it hard for, you know, your mechanic up the street to access what they need to fix your car.

John Deere, the tractor company, a real kind of corporate villain in the right-to-repair space, made it impossible for farmers to repair their combines, which, you know, makes it hard if it’s harvest season. You gotta wait for their dealer to come out and their repair shop to come out and fix it. There is an example in the book of the McDonald’s McFlurry. If you’ve ever wondered why you can always get french fries, but somehow the ice cream machine is always broken.

Well, it’s because Taylor Commercial Food Services, who owns the McFlurry machines, doesn’t let McDonald’s franchisees repair them themselves. So, you know, lots of these types of examples in the book, and, you know, thankfully there is, I think, a really burgeoning consumer movement around what we call the right to repair your own stuff. It’s run by a guy named Nathan Proctor at U.S. PIRG, the Public Interest Research Group, and they’ve had some big wins, including some memorandums of understanding with John Deere and even some movement at the federal level from the Federal Trade Commission on John Deere.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yeah, my experience with toner and printer was, one day I was about to order yet another cartridge for an HP laser printer, and I’m like, wait a second, I’ve paid something like 5x the cost of this printer. Let me use AI to find what’s a better alternative. And I ended up with, I went from an HP, I think it was an HP inkjet, to a Brother laser, unless I have it backwards, a Brother inkjet, whatever it was. The cartridges are like a fraction of the cost of the unit and are likely to be around that way for a long time.

But there was a thing a while ago where you could buy these just generic printer toner refills, and when HP figured that out, they would brick your printer, meaning it would just freeze and be dead. And that was it. How much control over our devices do manufacturers have, and what could we do about that?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah, I mean, technically it’s illegal to void your warranty if you repair your own stuff. But we see examples all the time of companies threatening to void your warranty if you make repairs. So that’s one sort of form of retribution companies can impose. There are also some examples in the book of things like, you know, the Keurig coffee machine not working if you insert a non-Keurig brand cup, or the K-Cup, you know, or the GE refrigerator no longer spitting out water if you use a non-GE water filter.
Things like that. And, you know, there’s been a lot of litigation in this space, which has been helpful in kind of, I think, pushing back against some of this corporate overreach.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: Huh, really interesting. Let’s talk about the power of public backlash. I remember not too long ago BMW proposed making the heated seats, like, a monthly subscription. I called my local dealer and said, “Cancel my deposits and gimme my money back. Cancel that deal. Take me off your list. You lost me as a BMW customer.” I’m wondering — and then there was an issue with Wendy’s with some of their pricing shenanigans. How significant is public backlash?

LINDSAY OWENS: Hugely, hugely significant. I mean, I really think one of the quickest ways that we can discipline companies who go too far with their pricing practices is to scream and yell and, like, share and tweet, right? It is absolutely the case that consumer backlash is a powerful force in convincing companies to go in a different direction. Voting with your wallet matters.

And throughout history, we’ve seen so many examples of consumer backlash really changing corporate behavior. One of the examples I love to talk about, which I include in the book, is, you know, actually in the mid-1990s, the CEO of Coke said in an offhanded interview to a Brazilian magazine that Coke was piloting installing thermometers in their vending machines — again, this was in the nineties — to hike the price of a Coke on a hot day. And he said he thought it was reasonable people would pay more on a hot day for an icy cold Coke out of the vending machine.

And it was the shot heard around the world. It was on the cover of every major newspaper. People were ticked about this, and they immediately had to walk it back. I mean, Pepsi really seized on the PR gaffe and, you know, saw their moment for an advantage, and Coke walked it back. And we saw that happen with Delta. Their partnership with Fetcherr was revealed by my organization, and, you know, Southwest and American jumped on it.

And I think that was a big part of why Delta walked back some of their plans. Obviously with the Instacart study my organization helped conduct, you know, consumer backlash was critical there. Two weeks later, you know, corporate issued a letter saying they would not use these practices. So I actually do think the quickest way to immediate action, by far, is consumer backlash.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: So let’s talk about a couple of companies that you spotlight as doing things right, like maintaining a cap on markups or freezing prices. One of the most obvious examples that comes to mind is Costco, pretty much universally beloved by their clients. What are they doing right?

LINDSAY OWENS: Yeah. So Costco is a little bit of a tricky example, but I use it in the book because I still think it’s a good one. I mean, their business model is a little different. They make a lot of their money from the subscription, the membership that you pay to shop in Costco.

But they do have a threshold on how much markup they will charge above their input costs. And they cap it at, I think it’s 14%. It depends. It varies a little if it’s a generic product, one of their own products, or if it’s a third-party product, but it’s a cost-plus pricing model.

They also designed a sensor suite that can rapidly estimate the robot’s position and orientation without relying on an offboard motion capture system, and a miniature electronics package to securely hold the tiny computational components on the nimble vehicle. “This is a really important milestone for the research community. This is the first demonstration of an aerial microrobot that is sensory and compute autonomous. There are many situations, like pollination or industrial surveillance, where you can’t use a larger robot. Small-scale robots are uniquely positioned for these types of tasks, and if this thread of technology becomes successful in the future, it could be very promising,” says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-corresponding author of a paper on the robot. He is joined on the paper by co-lead authors and MIT graduate students Yi-Hsuan (Nemo) Hsiao, Quang Phuc Kieu, and Zhongtao Guan; co-corresponding authors Jonathan P. How, a Ford Professor of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) and the Aerospace Controls Laboratory (ACL) at MIT; Elizabeth Farrell Helbling, an assistant professor at Cornell University; and others at MIT. The research appears today in Science Robotics. Increasing the payload The MIT researchers previously developed a swift, agile aerial microrobot with four wings, each powered by a set of soft actuators, or artificial muscles, that flap the wings rapidly so the bot can perform detailed maneuvers.  The robot, roughly the same size and shape as a microcassette, weighs less than a paperclip. To bring this tiny robot closer to real-world applications, the researchers need it to carry the additional weight from electronics for onboard sensing and computation, while still being fast, maneuverable, and robust to collisions. In this research, they developed a method to scale up the artificial muscles without hampering the robot’s performance. They carefully tuned the radius and length of the soft actuators, increasing their size by 50 percent while boosting the robot’s net lift forces by 46 percent.  “It is very difficult to scale up the actuators without causing the output power of the system to go down, which reduces the lift forces. We tuned the geometry of the robot very precisely so lift proportionally increases with the additional actuator weight,” Chen explains.  They were able to achieve a lift-to-weight ratio of 1.9, giving the robot more than enough lift force to carry the onboard electronics package they developed, which weighs only 244 milligrams.  The tiny electronics package contains the sensors, and microcontroller needed for onboard sensing and computation.  The researchers incorporated an inertial measurement unit to estimate attitude, an optical flow sensor to estimate lateral flight speed and position, and a time-of-flight sensor to measure height. But without the precision of the attached motion capture system, the robot does not know its absolute position, causing it to drift off course. Speedy sensing To overcome this challenge, the team designed a sensing algorithm to calculate the robot orientation, angular velocity, and position extremely quickly, simplifying the calculations to reduce the computational cost. They found that estimating position continuously at a faster rate yielded higher performance than a more accurate, slower estimation. “We spent a lot of time optimizing the selection of the sensors and position estimators so the robot would have very low drift. Our robot can now fly with positional accuracy that is comparable to flying with offboard cameras,” says Hsiao.  They integrated the sensors and computing components into a tiny electronics package, which they attached to a fiberglass substrate so it wouldn’t be thrown off by vibrations of the robot. “When you are talking about a computer which is that small, everything must be thought through carefully. There are so many factors to consider; it must do both perception and control, while fitting onto the robot and running fast enough that the vehicle will remain stable during flight,” How says. They tested the offboard computation capabilities of the aerial microrobot through a series of flight demonstrations, including hovering at different heights and following point-to-point trajectories. The robot maneuvered quickly and precisely, with positional errors of only a few centimeters. In addition, they demonstrated the robot’s potential for artificial pollination by using a joystick to send high-level position setpoints, guiding the aerial vehicle around several plants before carefully landing on a sunflower.  “This is quite difficult to do, even if you do have a motion-capture system,” Hsiao says. The researchers analyzed the vehicle’s power expenditures and found the electronics only consume about 6 percent of the total power, with the rest fueling the robot’s artificial muscles and wings.  They identified ways to further reduce power consumption from the electronics. This would allow for the addition of more components, like a camera that would enable the robot to recognize objects. The researchers are now working toward two goals: putting a camera onboard for autonomous object recognition and obstacle avoidance; and integrating power electronics and batteries onto the tiny robot, which would enable untethered flight in an outdoor environment.  This research was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), U.S. Office of Naval Research, U.S. Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and a Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

8fd900d387a7f388: Getting information does not equate to accessing justice
Originally published on Global Voices
Image courtesy the Hague Institute for Innovation in Law
By Zainab Malik

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine a woman facing eviction who turns to an AI chatbot for help. It explains her rights and drafts a letter to her landlord. But she cannot afford a lawyer, does not know where to submit the letter and has no institution that can enforce her rights fairly. The chatbot has made the law easier to understand, but has it brought her any closer to justice?

A September 2026 study by UK organization JUSTICE and the Administrative Fairness Lab found that one in six UK respondents who had experienced a legal dispute had used an AI chatbot. Researchers examined 77 conversations involving questions about rights, legal correspondence, complaints and court proceedings. Yet they could not establish whether these interactions helped resolve the disputes. We know more about how people use AI for legal help than whether it changes their circumstances.

That distinction matters. An estimated 1.5 billion people worldwide cannot obtain justice for their problems. HiiL’s Justice Needs Surveys, covering more than 150,000 people across 20 countries, show that only around four in 10 achieve a fair resolution. AI could help address this gap, but it is important to understand where its contribution begins and ends.
The promise of AI for justice seekers

People facing legal problems may not know whether what happened to them is unlawful, where to seek help or how to navigate an unfamiliar process. Legal advice is expensive, services can be difficult to reach, and institutions intimidating.

Purpose-built AI tools can explain rights clearly, organize information, prepare documents and identify relevant services. Voice-based tools may also reach people with limited literacy or without smartphones or reliable internet.

Early pilots are yielding promising results. In Australia, Hear Me Out, developed by the National Justice Project and the University of New South Wales, helps people identify the appropriate complaints body, understand the process and prepare supporting documents. Its pilot assisted more than 400 complaints, helping people turn experiences of injustice into complaints that can be pursued. In Nigeria, Citizens’ Gavel’s Podus AI helps people understand their legal rights, draft petitions and complaints, and identify the government agencies responsible for addressing them. Since its launch in March 2024, the platform has onboarded more than 33,000 users.
These are meaningful developments. But the number of tools and people assisted tells us only part of the story. What happens after someone submits a complaint?
When an answer is not a resolution

Understanding rights does not mean being able to exercise them. A tenant may know an eviction is unlawful but have nowhere to turn; a small business owner may prepare a claim but lack the means to pursue it. A person experiencing domestic abuse may face practical, financial or safety barriers to seeking protection.

Another challenge is getting the other party to participate. In dispute resolution, this is known as the “submission problem,” a concept developed by economists William Landes and Richard Posner. A process works only if both parties are willing to negotiate, accept mediation, or submit to a third-party decision. AI may help prepare a claim, but it cannot persuade a landlord to negotiate, compel an employer to pay wages, or make a business respond. Even when parties reach an agreement, there is no guarantee it will be respected. Without mechanisms to support compliance and enforce outcomes, an agreement on paper may have little practical effect.

There is also a growing challenge for the institutions receiving complaints. AI may make it much easier for people to submit them, potentially increasing demand on already overstretched public services. Recent UK reporting describes public bodies, councils and courts receiving a growing volume of AI-assisted submissions, some lengthy, repetitive and difficult to assess. Dubbed “AI clog,” the issue is not that more people are complaining — lowering barriers to redress is positive. The problem is that institutions may lack the capacity and resources to respond.

If AI increases the number of people approaching public authorities, those authorities must be equipped to meet the demand. This requires more than using AI to summarize documents or automate responses. It means better-designed complaints processes, adequately resourced institutions, trained staff and clear pathways for handling cases. Otherwise, technology risks making it easier to submit a complaint without making public services any more responsive.
Who owns the service?

Sustainability is another concern. A HiiL policy brief highlights the dependence of AI tools on external providers, proprietary platforms and uncertain funding. If a provider withdraws a service, what happens to the people relying on it?

HiiL’s exploration of voice-based AI support for local justice actors in Niger illustrates this risk. The aim was to make legal information available in local languages and support community intermediaries. But technology embedded in proprietary infrastructure can be difficult to maintain or transfer when a provider withdraws.

Ownership and governance therefore cannot be afterthoughts. Local justice providers and institutions need control over their tools, legal knowledge and data, as well as the resources to maintain and adapt services. Otherwise, technology intended to improve justice delivery may create new dependencies and disappear when people need it.
Making AI work for people seeking justice

AI for justice should be measured by more than chatbots launched, queries answered or documents generated. We need evidence that tools help people prevent problems, reach appropriate services, secure the participation of other parties and achieve fair outcomes.

This requires investment in tools designed around people’s problems and the providers best placed to address them. AI should connect users to human assistance, complement formal and informal justice mechanisms, and be supported by safeguards, accountability and sustainable financing. Crucially, public institutions must also be equipped to handle the increased demand that easier complaints procedures may generate. Evaluation should ask whether AI improves outcomes, for whom, under what conditions and at what cost. AI can make legal help more accessible and help people take action. But its promise will depend on whether the wider justice system can respond.

The ambition should not be to give everyone a free AI lawyer while leaving them waiting for an answer from the institutions responsible for upholding their rights. It should be to use technology to help those institutions work better, address people’s needs and deliver on their responsibilities fairly and effectively.
Zainab Malik is Senior Policy and Advocacy Advisor at HiiL.
Written by The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL)

d6fcfae4390a55c9: Waymo has suspended driverless freeway rides across the US after California regulators intervened over robotaxis entering construction zones and trying to bypass highway patrol vehicles.
California's DMV banned Waymo from offering driverless trips on its freeways on Wednesday, November 11. The same day, Waymo pulled the handbrake on its freeway services countrywide.

The move affects all areas in which Waymo operates on freeways, including San Francisco, Los Angeles, Miami, Phoenix, and Austin. The Alphabet-owned company has not indicated how long the suspension will last. Waymo says freeway testing will continue with trained specialists behind the wheel.

Jonathan Groveman, spokesperson for the California DMV, told the Associated Press that the organization imposed the ban following two incidents involving Waymo's robotaxis that posed an "imminent hazard to public safety."
On November 5, three of the company's driverless cars entered an active construction zone on US 101 near Burlingame, south of San Francisco.

The second incident occurred the following day, and in footage shared widely online, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to drive around highway patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break – a maneuver used to slow or stop traffic.

"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," Groveman said in the statement.
Groveman said the DMV had already imposed restrictions and required corrective action following similar incidents on May 18.
Waymo subsequently recalled nearly 4,000 cars after some were caught ignoring road closure signs and cones designating construction zones in Phoenix and San Francisco.
A separate recall covered software affecting nearly 3,800 robotaxis over problems including slowing on high-speed roadways and driving into floodwater.
A Waymo spokesperson said that despite California's temporary ban, its robotaxis continue to operate on city streets across the US.

"Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," they said. "Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state.

"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week.
"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations."
Other nuisances and hazards caused by errant Waymos include clogging traffic in thick fog, driving into telephone poles, and killing cats and dogs. ®

fe1c78ae1f59c2d8: Microsoft’s official agent framework package hosted on PyPI has been hijacked and now installs info-stealing malware, multiple security research firms have discovered.

CEO Satya Nadella may be on stage trying to wow investors and customers at his company’s annual Ignite conference, but somewhere in the bowels of a building in Redmond his open source team is likely panicking at what appears to be unauthorized access to an administrator account on Microsoft’s Github organization.

The problem package is Microsoft’s agent-framework, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, researchers reported late yesterday and this morning. According to OX Security, version 1.26.1 was reverted to a safe version, but the attacker later uploaded 1.26.2 through Microsoft’s official PyPI publisher account, suggesting that, at least at the time of their report, the credentials hadn’t been locked down.
Safe to say, but if you find either version in your environment assume you have some account security work to do.

Microsoft agent-framework for Python boasts nearly 200,000 downloads a month and is used to build and deploy AI agents. As of those latest releases, it’s also being used to exfiltrate environment variables, credential files, and other secrets for Azure, Git, Docker, Hugging Face, and other sensitive developer services.

To make matters worse, the package never needs to be imported to do its dirty work – all it takes is a Python interpreter with the package installed to start up – the infected package still pulls the genuine 1.26.0 version of Microsoft’s agent-framework in order to keep itself running and looking legitimate, while in the background it gathers up credentials, encrypts them as a base64-encoded chunk of JSON, and sends them off to a webhook.site address hard coded into the malware.

It appears from researcher accounts that this is made to act fast, as the malware isn’t persistent and only runs as long as the malicious version of the agent-framework remains in a site-packages directory. What it does do, however, is not just look for credentials in the environment: It actually starts calling for new ones and collecting them, too.
In particular, the malware requests fresh identity tokens from GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, and Azure itself, which are exfiltrated to the same webhook site.

“That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away,” said researchers at OpenSourceMalware.

The agent-framework GitHub repo is offline as of writing. It’s been pointed out online that Microsoft’s repo for ONNX Runtime, an AI accelerator, is also offline. Other Microsoft repos remain available, and neither Microsoft nor security researchers have linked the ONNX repo’s pull to the malware campaign.

“We have made some repositories private while we investigate malicious content,” a Microsoft spokesperson told The Register. “Our priority is to protect customers and the broader ecosystem. We are working to review and will take further action as needed.”®
Updated at 1805 with comment from Microsoft.
c1576f35931e9ffc: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform.

The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications.
It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability.

Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020, then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency.
Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price.
But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users?

In a blog post, the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure."
The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support.
MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together.

MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part.

Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem, promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level.

SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system.
Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it.

MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture.

MongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications. The idea was to accelerate those queries without changing the document structure or moving data to another system.
Firebolt gives MongoDB another tool for a familiar job: making analytics feel at home beside its operational database. Whether the plumbing lives up to the pitch remains to be seen. ®

24b01c999fdbd7da: Be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice.

Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning.
Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze.

Sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges users to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background.

The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again.
"After hitting my $200 Ultra plan limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads."
There didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made.

They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy.

"I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation."
The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond.
It's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader said, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app.
"I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits."

Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong, just with customer requests.

The problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud, and it appears the lessons need to be learned again.
Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we're paying for and to reach a human when the numbers don’t add up."
Caution is advised. Especially when a service appears to need only a few more dollars of credit to finish off that task. ®

43fa5cd5b871a557: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021.

Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next.
The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds.
Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith
In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex, the familiar list of requirements came up first:
Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts
Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint
A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching.
Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise.

Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled.

So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it.
Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery
Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones.

Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000.

Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully.
Where you recover is the other half

Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it.

Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone.
Meeting all of this is harder than it looks
Put the pieces together and the bar is high:
Backups you have actually tested
Recovery times you can state and meet
And a clean, separate place to recover to

Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations.
Where cloud disaster recovery fits

Cloud-native disaster recovery changes the equation. Cove’s DRaaS solution lets teams stage a pre-recovered VM in the N-able cloud that can be failed over to in about 15 minutes, off the production network. That answers the speed question and the location question together. Forensic investigators can validate and hunt in the sandbox while the business keeps moving, with rollback to earlier points in time. Once everyone agrees the recovery point is clean, workloads can run from the cloud over VPN, and failback uses recovery agents to bring changes home.
Where to start

Insurance is a financial failsafe, not a substitute for a bad data protection posture. Start by listing what the business couldn’t lose for 72 hours, set recovery targets, test them and document the results. Check the policy itself: a standalone cyber policy rather than a small add-on to a general one, with a limit of at least $1 million, and $2 million as the business scales. And if an incident does hit, disconnect affected machines from the network rather than powering them off, so forensic data survives.

1399dbcd49f917d6: Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement.

It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, "be removed from a future version of Windows," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default.
After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties.
PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless.

PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover, who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude.

PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain.

The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time.

Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts.

Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft.
Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself.
"Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead.
Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®

1d09732fd76edc74: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences.

For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption?

These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one.
Making recovery part of the defence

This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible.
Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite.

InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery.

The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed.

For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery.
Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions.

Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences.
For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation.

301f7eaa368f4124: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there.

Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union.

A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto.

Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good.

Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs).

Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register: "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it.

"We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with."

Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said.
Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

Earlier, local government committee chairman Mansor Zakaria told the assembly the local councils were examining the available provisions in deciding whether to grant licences to betting outlets.
These include rules related to town planning and zoning, public safety, health, public nuisance, traffic flow, and compliance with building regulations, he said.
Mansor was replying to Kota Darul Aman assemblyman Teh Swee Leong, who asked what the state planned to do following the court decision.
Sanusi also defended the collection of RM283,676 in public donations through Yayasan Kedah Sejahtera to help the state pay RM50,000 in court costs arising from the case.
The collection had been questioned by Teh, a DAP assemblyman, who asked why a welfare foundation was being used to pay the government's legal costs, and whether its constitution permitted this.
He also asked what would happen to the remaining RM233,676.
Sanusi said the foundation, which he described as an NGO, collected the contributions from the public before passing them to the state.
He said direct contributions to the government would have required official receipts, making the arrangement through the NGO more convenient.
He said the remaining donations would be used for other gambling-related cases still before the courts.

06d2778da6d620f1: Ticket resale giant StubHub International has warned customers that a recent breach may have exposed their personal information to cybercriminals.

The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond.
