97482236c183a9f1: SHENZHEN: Xi Jinping's personal welcome to US President Donald Trump at Shenzhen airport on Wednesday for a summit made him China's first paramount leader in decades to greet a foreign counterpart on arrival.
After Air Force One touched down, Trump descended to the red carpet, where President Xi himself was waiting to greet him.
The men shared a brief hug before walking together to their cars beside a crowd of cheering performers waving pom-poms.

It stood out among other world leaders' arrivals in Shenzhen this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting, where Xi, Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin will hold historic three-way talks on Thursday.
Putin, who arrived in the early hours of Wednesday, was met by Xi's right-hand man Cai Qi.

But Trump's personal welcome is believed to be the first by a paramount leader in China in decades – and marks an upgrade to his high-profile summit trip to Beijing in May, when vice-president Han Zheng was there to meet him.
Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, said Trump was "visibly delighted by Xi's gesture".

"Given Beijing's overriding objective of extending the fragile calm in the US-China relationship for as long as possible, Xi will look for opportunities to extend courtesy and respect to Trump during his visit, like he did in greeting Trump on the tarmac upon arrival," Hass told AFP.
"It set a positive tone for Trump's visit, marking a contrast from the swirl of news around the Jensen Huang scandal that preceded Trump's arrival in Shenzhen."
Huang resigned last week as CEO of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia after admitting to an affair, reportedly with a woman some US officials suspect to be a Chinese spy.
Xi's warm greeting of Trump was also reciprocal.
When Xi travelled to the US in May, the US leader also met him on arrival, reportedly the first American president in decades to do so, if visits from the Pope are not included.

Xi told Trump on the tarmac on Wednesday that during his state visit to the US, the "presidential couple came to the airport in person and hosted a grand welcome ceremony", according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Xi also noted that "China is a nation with a tradition of courtesy that values reciprocating goodwill", the Xinhua report said.
Although several other leaders arriving in Shenzhen for the Apec summit got cheering crowds or bouquets of flowers, one arrival stood out for its relative lack of ceremony.
Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi was greeted not by a top minister but by military guards and a woman whom Japanese media named as the Chinese foreign ministry's ambassador of protocol.

Long-frosty ties between the countries have worsened since Takaichi suggested last year that Japan could intervene militarily in any conflict over Taiwan, the democratic island Beijing claims as its territory.
Meanwhile, Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum travelled on a commercial flight, as she often does as part of an austerity policy.
5921bee27cca2ad6: MANCHESTER: Mauricio Pochettino arrived at Manchester United on Wednesday morning, after an overnight flight took their new manager from his final match in charge of the US team into a relegation battle at a club desperately seeking a revival in fortunes.
Pochettino posted a photo of Manchester from the air on Instagram, signalling the end of his seven-hour journey from Cincinnati.
A private plane had whisked him away shortly after the US beat Haiti on Tuesday, and the 54-year-old Argentine was driven straight to United's training centre at Carrington.
Pochettino has precious little time to settle into his new surroundings, however, with an away Premier League game at arch-rivals Liverpool looming large on Sunday.

United announced Pochettino's appointment on Friday, following Michael Carrick's sacking, with the manager delaying his arrival to lead the US in their two-legged CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final.

His focus must swiftly switch from international football to the daily grind of club management, where a harsh spotlight will follow his every move and a drastic change in form is needed, and quickly.

United have not won the league title since 2013, when long-serving manager Alex Ferguson retired, and the 20-times English champions have registered one win in 10 league games this season to lie 18th in the table, their lowest position at this stage of a top-flight campaign since 1986-87.
That was the season Ferguson took charge, and 40 years later Pochettino arrives in similar circumstances.

Ferguson was given time at United, whose wait for another league title had reached almost two decades upon his arrival. Two days after taking charge, Ferguson's side lost at Oxford United and dropped into the relegation zone.
Manchester United finished 11th that season, and had to wait until 1993 for Ferguson to deliver the title, although he did win a European Cup Winners' Cup, FA Cup and League Cup along the way.
Pochettino, whose only league title as a manager came at Paris St Germain, is unlikely to be afforded such patience.
US midfielder DaMarcus Beasley, who spent a season on-loan at Manchester City, joked with Pochettino in a post-game interview on TNT Sports on Tuesday that "Manchester will always be blue."
"No way, you will see," Pochettino replied.
"Give me time, give me time and that is going to start to change, for sure." - Reuters

bb2c7bdfdad2f6ba: Nvidia's board says it has no plans to bring Jensen Huang back as the GPU giant reports quarterly revenue more than double that of a year ago.

The AI infrastructure leviathan had some reassuring to do after its leather-jacketed rockstar leader left under a cloud last week. Huang had been central to its rise as the dominant supplier of AI compute.
Newly appointed board chair Harvey Jones ruled out an imminent comeback, saying: "The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
Jones said the board was addressing the fallout and strengthening oversight, pointing to the creation of a committee to scrutinize the firm's security policies and export compliance.
Nvidia has also retained the services of talent spotters Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new leader, according to Jones.

Interim CEO and chief financial officer Colette Kress struck an upbeat tone on the company's Q3 earnings call. The results gave her plenty to work with: revenue rose 103 percent to $115.8 billion, while operating income climbed 115 percent to $77.5 billion.

"We're addressing strong demand for compute across a diverse and expansive set of end customers, including hyperscalers, frontier labs, AI natives, enterprises, and governments," Kress said. She raised Nvidia's outlook for fiscal 2028, saying that the firm now expects revenue to grow approximately 75 percent year-on-year.
Analysts immediately questioned this, asking what gave Kress the confidence to raise the outlook, given all the uncertainty surrounding the future direction of the company.
Kress cited growing demand and additional supply as reasons for lifting the fiscal 2028 growth forecast from 70 to 75 percent.
When asked about the financing deals that Nvidia provides for some of its customers, Kress appeared to hint that some things might change.

"Our neoclouds have been so instrumental in terms of both supporting enterprises and supporting many of the different countries around the world, particularly on the sovereign perspective. And we continue to be working with them," she stated.

But she added: "I think we would look at this and take a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing, as a lot of things have changed over this last quarter... but we do have some very, very strong existing customers that we will be continuing to work with."

Kress also said that Nvidia's rack-scale Rubin platform had generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments. She said the firm expects the major frontier AI labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its Data Center revenue this year.

Kress said that Nvidia is no longer shipping licensed products based on its Hopper silicon to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to advanced AI technology, and so its future guidance does not count on any Hopper revenue from there.
Nvidia sold $2.4 billion worth of Hopper kit to China during Q3 after being given the go-ahead from the Trump administration to sell products like its H200 accelerators in China.
Analysts say they expect doubts to remain over Nvidia's future despite the strong Q3 results as the quarter was already in the bag by the time the Huang scandal broke.

"Nvidia's next battle is not against competitors alone. It must navigate export controls, sovereign AI initiatives, supply chain expansion, and rising capital intensity – all while protecting industry-leading margins," commented Forrester principal analyst Naveen Chhabra.

"The market sees the biggest risk not in the financials, but the leadership and employee motivation amidst turmoil, which began only after the Q3 ended. The bigger risk is not near-term demand but operations, maintaining employee confidence, retaining talent, and preserving Nvidia's innovation culture."

February's results should offer a clearer view of Nvidia after Huang. For now, the mighty AI platform biz expects another record quarter, forecasting revenue of $130 billion, give or take 3 percent. ®

ff3e9d2b55b8b967: SHAH ALAM: The Sultan of Selangor, Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah, has expressed admiration for the establishment of the Merdeka Textile Museum and its role in preserving and showcasing the rich textile heritage of the Malay world.

In a Selangor Royal Office Facebook post, Sultan Sharafuddin said he was particularly impressed by the museum's curatorial standards and the meticulous arrangement and presentation of its collection of fabrics, traditional attire and textiles.

His Royal Highness was also drawn to the museum's efforts to showcase the intricacy of traditional craftsmanship and explore the history, culture and identity of the Malay and Nusantara communities through textiles.
"I am greatly impressed by the establishment of the Merdeka Textile Museum and its role in highlighting the history, artistry and craftsmanship of traditional Malay textiles.
"I had hoped that a similar textile museum would have been established in Selangor by now, but I am disappointed that this has yet to materialise," the Sultan said.
Yesterday, Sultan Sharafuddin, accompanied by Tengku Permaisuri of Selangor Tengku Permaisuri Norashikin, spent almost two hours touring the museum, which was officially launched on Aug 21.
Among the exhibits that particularly fascinated the Sultan was the personal collection of the late cultural figure Azah Aziz, which forms the core of the museum's collection.

Donated by her family, the collection comprises 240 pieces of traditional attire and 69 traditional accessories, including songket sarongs, baju kurung limar and gold-thread embroidery, preserving her legacy in safeguarding Malay traditional clothing heritage.

Located at Look at 118, within the Merdeka 118 precinct in Kuala Lumpur, next to Stadium Merdeka, the museum was developed by PNB Merdeka Ventures and carries the theme 'The Malay World in Threads and Tales'.

"Supplies of petroleum products continue to increase despite several constraints that could affect market price stability.
"Geopolitical uncertainties and the risk of disruptions to petroleum shipments could still affect global supplies.
"As such, global petroleum prices are expected to remain volatile in the near term," it said.
MOF said the Madani government remained committed to protecting the public and businesses through targeted fuel subsidies under the Budi Madani initiative.
Nearly RM4 billion has been allocated for fuel subsidies next year to help ease the people's cost-of-living burden.
Under Budi95, eligible recipients will continue to enjoy RON95 at RM1.99 per litre, compared with the unsubsidised price of RM3.72.
This means the government subsidises RM1.73 per litre, or 47 per cent of the unsubsidised price.
For Budi Diesel, eligible recipients will continue paying RM2.10 per litre, compared with the unsubsidised price of RM4.72.
The government bears a subsidy of RM2.67 per litre, equivalent to 56 per cent of the unsubsidised price.
MOF said eligible Malaysians could continue purchasing subsidised RON95 and diesel using their MyKad under Budi95 and Budi Diesel, subject to their respective monthly eligibility limits.
"The Madani government will continue taking a prudent approach to protect the public from price fluctuations while ensuring the country's fuel supply remains sufficient and secure," it said.
528841cbf861a044: Most staples for Thanksgiving, including potatoes and cranberries, haven't jumped in price this year. Noah Samuel Franz on UnsplashInflation-weary Americans have at least some good news to cheer this holiday season: The cost of a basic Thanksgiving meal has stabilized. A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people clocks in at US$78.93, approximately 0.4% less than in 2025, according to the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute. That’s because most staples haven’t seen a sharp jump in prices. Americans are still justified in feeling stressed about high grocery bills, but it’s because of the cumulative effect of rising prices in recent years. While inflation has slowed since its peak of more than 9% in 2022, the cost of a Thanksgiving meal is roughly 25% higher than it was before the COVID-19 pandemic began. I’m an agricultural economist who has been studying the many drivers of food inflation. What’s key to remember is that inflation data tells us how quickly prices are increasing, not whether prices are returning to previous levels. So even modest price jumps today are layered on already-elevated prices. Here’s what Americans can expect when they go shopping for Thanksgiving, from turkey to dessert: Go for frozen turkey Stable frozen turkey prices have played an important role in keeping overall holiday meal costs close to last year’s levels. The average advertised price for a frozen turkey over 16 pounds (about 7 kilograms) was $0.96 per pound, essentially unchanged from the $0.97 per pound in the same period last year, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Turkey Report, published on Nov. 13, 2026. These prices reflect the typical discounts leading up to Thanksgiving, when retailers often cut turkey prices as part of their holiday promotions. It’s a different story with fresh turkey prices, which are about 11% higher than a year ago, according to the Department of Agriculture data. So shoppers seeking a fresh bird may face a higher grocery bill. A longer-term trend is that turkey consumption has gradually declined over time. As a result, the cost of Thanksgiving depends on much more than turkey prices alone. This is where side dishes come in. Frozen turkey is among the Thanksgiving staples that haven’t seen big price jumps this past year. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh A mixed picture for side dishes Mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce and sweet potato casserole are among the dishes that a frugal shopper might consider. Sweet potatoes are 12.5% cheaper year on year, and cranberry prices have dropped 4.8%, according to the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service’s Weekly Grocery Store Specialty Crops data. Potato prices, meanwhile, have been stable, increasing just 1.1% over the past year, according to September’s consumer price index, the most recent month of full data. If you’re considering mac and cheese, the costs of the main ingredients should balance out: Pasta and cornmeal prices are 4.3% higher year on year, while cheese is 3% cheaper. Prices for fruits and vegetables, however, have mostly ticked upward and are 3.9% higher than a year ago. That includes green beans, which are 2.2% more expensive. Prices for fresh apples are up 7.5%, and up 2.6% for lettuce. More broadly, higher prices for some fresh vegetables reflect the cost pressures facing food production. Farmers are grappling with high fertilizer, fuel and transportation expenses, not to mention tariffs in certain sectors. Of course, Thanksgiving isn’t complete without regional traditions. Sauerkraut is a popular side dish for turkey in the mid-Atlantic states, but fans will have to pay substantially more. Cabbage is about 30% more expensive year on year due to weather shocks and pest outbreaks that have reduced supply. Sauerkraut, a popular side dish in mid-Atlantic states, is likely to be pricier amid higher cabbage prices. Kelsey Todd on Unsplash Don’t forget dessert Americans might also find some sweet relief in prices for popular desserts. Some key baking staples became more affordable. Butter prices have fallen 10.3% over the previous year, while flour is down by 1.1% and sugar by 1%, according to the September consumer price index data. But some of the biggest savings come from eggs, where prices have dropped sharply. Like the turkey industry, egg production was hard-hit in 2022 by a highly pathogenic avian flu outbreak, which reduced supplies and pushed prices up. Since then, producers have rebuilt flocks and expanded production to grow supply. Egg prices are now 20.3% lower than a year ago. Where consumers will shell out more is milk, up 2.3%; canned fruit, up 2.3%; and frozen bakery products, up 1.3%, according to the consumer price index data. Pumpkins for pie-making will cost 2% more than last year. So keep all this in mind if you plan to bake a pie. And if you opt for a store-bought pumpkin pie, expect to pay about 2.5% more. Where other savings can be found Shoppers looking for alternatives to turkey could head to the poultry aisle. Prices for whole fryer and roaster chickens are anywhere from 7% to 20% lower than a year ago, according to USDA grocery store price data. Consumers can also take advantage of Thanksgiving promotions offered by grocery retailers. Several major retailers offer complete Thanksgiving meal baskets for less than $40, which can translate to approximately $3.50 to $4 per person. Among major retailers, Walmart is advertising its Thanksgiving basket for 10 people at $35, Aldi at $39 for 10 people and Target at $30 for six people. Although the contents vary, these meal packages generally include Thanksgiving favorites such as turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce, and ingredients for green bean and potato side dishes. Inflation remains at the top of consumers’ minds, and it isn’t expected to ease anytime soon. But in the case of Thanksgiving, shoppers can find at least some relief as they seek out staples for their feast. 6a0a067f39b92102: KUALA LUMPUR: Construction of Lynas' permanent disposal facility (PDF) has reached 79 per cent as of Oct 31, the Dewan Rakyat was told.
Deputy Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Datuk Dr Mohammad Yusof Apdal said 1.46 million metric tonnes of WLP (water leach purification) residue has been transferred into it.
"The Atomic Energy Licensing Board (AELB) is regularly monitoring construction and Lynas' compliance with its licence conditions.
"The monitoring data can also be accessed in real time through mosti.gov.my and jta.gov.my," he said when winding up the debate on his ministry's Budget 2027 allocation at the committee stage.
WLP residue is a byproduct generated during the extraction and chemical processing of rare earth elements (REEs).

He said that, in the first five years of the extension, Lynas was required to modify facilities at the Lynas Advanced Materials Plant in Gebeng to lower the radioactivity concentration of WLP residue below the control limit under the Act.
Lynas has submitted planning documents to modify its cracking and leaching process using the Low Temperature Leaching method, he said.
Yusof said any rare earth processing activity involving naturally occurring radioactive material above 1 becquerel per gram was subject to AELB regulation and licensing under the Act.

It was reported that Malaysia had renewed Lynas Rare Earths' operating licence for another 10 years to import raw materials containing naturally occurring radioactive material and process rare earths, the Australian miner said on Monday.
Shares of Lynas rose as much as seven per cent to A$20.30 by 0131 GMT, hitting their highest level since Oct 21, 2025, while the broader ASX 200 benchmark was down about 0.5 per cent.

f96db31816392fa7: PETALING JAYA: PKR tidak akan membelakangkan DAP demi memikat sokongan pengundi Melayu, kata Naib Presiden Dr Zaliha Mustafa ketika menolak cadangan menghidupkan semula kerjasama ala-Barisan Alternatif (BA).

"Mereka yang buat cadangan itu tidak melalui pengalaman tersebut, oleh itu telah buat cadangan yang pada saya tidak logik," katanya.
BA merupakan gabungan parti pembangkang yang ditubuhkan pada 1999 susulan gelombang gerakan Reformasi selepas pemecatan Anwar sebagai timbalan perdana menteri pada September 1998.

Gabungan itu pada asalnya menghimpunkan Parti Keadilan Nasional (kini PKR), PAS, DAP dan Parti Rakyat Malaysia (PRM) bagi menentang BN pada PRU 1999, sebelum DAP menarik diri pada 2001 susulan percanggahan pendirian berhubung isu penubuhan negara Islam oleh PAS.
1843453e6d2ff7c1: PETALING JAYA: A lawyer says there is nothing treasonous about the opposition by the attorney-general and the federal territories minister to former prime minister Najib Razak being under house arrest under a conditional pardon.

Zainul Rijal Abu Bakar said Attorney-General Dusuki Mokhtar and federal territories minister Hannah Yeoh were asked by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, who chairs the Federal Territories Pardons Board, to present their views.

“Expressing a different opinion, including disagreeing with a proposal, is part of their responsibility as board members, not an act of defiance or disloyalty towards the royal institution,” he said in a Facebook post.

He was commenting on the minutes of the Sept 18 FTPB meeting, circulated online today, which revealed that Dusuki and Yeoh had opposed to allowing Najib to serve the rest of his prison sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest.
According to the declassified minutes, the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, Sultan Ibrahim, decided to grant Najib a conditional pardon despite their objections.
The declassified minutes led some, including a former minister, to accuse Dusuki and Yeoh of disobeying the king.
Zainul, an adviser to the Malaysian Muslim Lawyers Association, said the Federal Constitution empowered the king to grant pardons.
He said the king did not necessarily have to accept the pardons board’s view.
“The views of the board members must be considered, but the decision on whether to exercise the power of pardon is the king’s prerogative,” he said.
Zainul also said there were limits to how far the courts could intervene in decisions involving the king's pardon powers.

Najib, who was convicted of corruption involving RM42 million in SRC International funds, was ordered by the High Court on Nov 10 to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, after his reduced RM50 million fine was settled by Umno.

5083447d6d326a74: KUALA LUMPUR: CR Kumar faces an early test of his credentials as national women's hockey coach, with the Speedy Tigresses needing a top-four finish at the Asian Champions Trophy (ACT) in Bhopal to meet the Malaysian Hockey Confederation's (MHC) target.
Malaysia open their campaign against defending champions India tomorrow, with the Asian Games champions expected to provide a stern examination of Kumar's side.
Kumar was appointed national women's hockey coach in April, with MHC setting a top-four finish in Asia as the target for the Indian coach.
His first assignment was the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games last month, where the Speedy Tigresses defeated Thailand 4-0 to finish fifth.
Malaysia have a bronze medal from the 2013 edition in Kakamigahara, Japan, where they defeated China 3-1.
However, their most recent ACT campaign in Rajgir, India, in 2024 ended with a fourth-place finish after a 4-1 defeat to Japan.
The challenge now is for Kumar's side to rise to the occasion in Bhopal and deliver the result MHC expects.

World No. 21 Malaysia face a formidable opening opponent in India, who are ranked seventh in the world and were crowned Asian Games champions last month to secure qualification for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
The match is effectively a clash between the SEA Games champions and Asian champions.
India, under head coach Sjoerd Marijne, will be favourites to claim their fourth ACT title after triumphs in 2016, 2023 and 2024.
Malaysia have faced India 21 times since the 2009 Asia Cup in Bangkok, losing 19 matches and drawing the other two.
The Speedy Tigresses will have their work cut out containing India's skilful forwards, including Navneet Kaur, Deepika, Beauty Dungdung, Lalremsiami and Mumtaz Khan.
Kumar said the Asian Games had provided valuable insights into his team's strengths and weaknesses, while also allowing them to study their opponents.
"Based on that experience, we have developed better game plans and strategies for this tournament.

"My goal is to see the players perform better than they did at the Asian Games, while aiming for better results. I want the players to draw upon all the experience they have gained and translate it into a more convincing performance in Bhopal," he said.

However, three players who featured at the Asian Games, namely Siti Zulaikha Husain, Iman Adawiyah Suhaimi and Anith Humaira Baharudin, have been left out as they continue their recovery from injuries.
They have been replaced by Dian Nursyakira Najwa Al Wadqa Nazeri, Nur Shafika Ahmad Kamil and Nur Zuha Qistina Ridzuan.
The tournament will follow a single round-robin format, with the top four teams advancing to the semi-finals.
After facing India, Malaysia will take on world No. 4 China on Nov 21, world No. 15 South Korea on Nov 22, world No. 11 Japan on Nov 24 and world No. 28 Thailand on Nov 25.
The semi-finals and final will be played on Nov 27 and 28 respectively.

82018f2597fc7bdc: SEMPORNA: Rising accommodation and diving package costs are making Semporna less competitive compared with international dive destinations, says a diver from Peninsular Malaysia.

Lester Yeoh said resort stays bundled with diving packages had increased significantly, from an average of RM700 per night during the Covid-19 lockdown, when overseas travel was restricted, to between RM1,200 and RM1,500 now.
"As a diver from Peninsular Malaysia, I think prices in Semporna have gone out of hand. With that amount of money, I can get a much better experience elsewhere," he told the New Straits Times.
He said resorts offering Sipadan diving packages generally required a minimum booking of three to four nights, but guests would get only one day of diving at the world-renowned island.
"Honestly, the rest of the islands are mediocre compared with Sipadan. That is not to say there is nothing interesting.

"If you are interested in turtles, Semporna is your best bet. But, as I mentioned, it does not justify the cost," he said, adding that a return flight from Kuala Lumpur to Tawau could cost between RM600 and RM700, while a five-day, four-night holiday would cost another RM6,000.

"With RM700 for flights and another RM6,000 for the trip, I might as well go for a seven-day, six-night liveaboard in the Maldives, where I can see much more pelagic marine life, enjoy a longer holiday and experience a different culture.

"Another option is the Phuket-Similan liveaboard, which costs about RM3,000 for five days and four nights, with cheaper flights. On the final day, I can enjoy Phuket's nightlife, Thai food and traditional massage."
Yeoh said Semporna would struggle to compete with international destinations if it did not offer visitors experiences beyond marine activities.
Diving instructor Denise Lim, who has worked with a dive operator based in Semporna, concurred that the district had experienced a recent slowdown in tourism demand.
She said the dive centre was usually fully booked during the Christmas and New Year holidays, but demand had been different since last year.
Lim also expressed concern over the deterioration of Sipadan's coral reefs, attributing some of the damage to divers with poor buoyancy control.
She recalled that when she first visited the island 10 years ago, schools of jackfish and barracuda formed seemingly endless walls beneath the waters.
"My most memorable working experience as an instructor here was diving with a school of about 40 to 50 hammerhead sharks at Sipadan.

"Now, they are just a very small school," she said, urging the authorities to step up ocean protection measures and calling on divers to help protect the reefs by avoiding touching or kicking corals and using reef-safe sunscreen.
Lim, who is leaving Semporna, said the place was not perfect, particularly in terms of hygiene, but she held the place and its people dear to her heart.
c1253c89a3ee647b: Microsoft has pushed Windows Server 2028 into public preview, with an eye on beefed-up security, new infrastructure support, and the inevitable nod to AI.

Neil Hinnant, a director on the Windows Server team, talked up the security tweaks. There's a hardened Server Core configuration by default and a new security baseline. "Trusted Launch extends protection to virtual machines," he wrote. "Confidential VM support begins a journey to support integrity-protected runtimes on supported CVM hardware."
Server Core will therefore arrive locked down by default – good news for security, potentially less so for administrators whose existing configurations depend on more permissive settings.

"For years, Windows Server shipped compatible by default," wrote Senior Product Manager Christina Curlette. "Making the server secure was up to you, usually by applying the Security Baseline or your own hardening scripts after setup."

With Windows Server 2028 (and starting from Windows Server Insider Preview build 29706), Server Core will be installed hardened. "Hundreds of security settings are on from first boot," Curlette wrote.

"Because the defaults are now locked down, some things that worked on Windows Server 2025 may not work on Windows Server 2028 without changes. This includes older protocols, legacy authentication, and some management tools and scripts."

For a company obsessed with backward compatibility, this is quite the step. Welcome though the hardening is, administrators will need to test carefully: working on Windows Server 2025 won't guarantee a smooth ride in the brave new world.

AI gets a role on both sides of the security fence: helping uncover vulnerabilities and giving Microsoft another reason to sell servers. Windows Server 2028 is being pitched for running models locally, with support for accelerators such as AMD's Instinct MI350P.

Not every server is destined to babysit a model, however, and the storage changes may be more immediately useful to enterprise administrators. Windows Server 2028 will enable native NVMe storage by default, along with NVMe over TCP and RDMA. Booting from ReFS is also planned, adding another item to the storage upgrade list.

Intune management for Windows Server has also entered preview. Azure Arc, with its cloud-native management workflows, is obviously still around, while Intune brings a more familiar management interface for administrators already using it for endpoints.

Hinnant acknowledged that this was a "major release," and it looks like the security hardening alone will require a good deal of thought from administrators before organizations adopt the eventual production release.

Esben Dochy, Principal Technical Evangelist for SecOps at Lansweeper, told The Register that Microsoft had indicated that the hardened security only applied to new installations. "If that remains in the final release," he said, "in-place upgrades could be easier. The catch is that those servers may also miss out on the new security defaults."
"Hardening is the right direction," he said, "but it will add work for teams moving to Server 2028."

According to Lansweeper’s figures, as of October 2026, Windows Server 2019 ruled the roost with 33 percent. Windows Server 2025 had reached just 7 percent. "From behavior we've seen in the past," said Dochy, "adoption is primarily driven by lifecycle, so until the more used versions start going EOL, I don't expect much adoption, similar to what Server 2025 is experiencing."

Windows Server 2025 remains under extended support until 2034, but Microsoft's direction of travel is clear: beefed-up security by default, a home for AI applications, and Intune management for fleets of servers. ®
de8df71fe312763a: PONTIAN: Suspected construction waste from Singapore has resurfaced at a previously closed dumping site in Rimba Terjun here, with 10 lorries linked to various companies detected during an enforcement operation.

Johor Solid Waste Management and Public Cleansing Corporation (SWCorp) director Zainal Fitri Ahmad said 8 of the lorries had records showing they entered Malaysia carrying stone waste, involving four companies.

"Checks conducted with the Customs Department's Import Division at the Sultan Abu Bakar Complex (KSAB) found that eight vehicles had entry records showing they had brought in loads of stone waste, involving four companies.
"The remaining two lorries had no corresponding Customs entry records, while checks also found an excavator and heaps of mixed waste at the site," he said.
Zainal, who led the enforcement operation at Lot 3700, Mukim Rimba Terjun, on Nov 13, said it followed public complaints about suspected illegal waste dumping.

He said ownership details of all 10 vehicles had been referred to the Road Transport Department for verification, while the landowner was being identified with the assistance of the Pontian Land Office.

An investigation paper will be opened under Section 71(1) of the Solid Waste and Public Cleansing Management Act 2007 (Act 672), which prohibits the unauthorised handling and disposal of controlled solid waste.
Those convicted face a fine of between RM10,000 and RM100,000, imprisonment of between six months and five years, or both.
Johor Local Government and Housing Committee chairman Datuk Jafni Md Shukor is scheduled to visit the site tomorrow at 4pm to assess the situation and review the latest developments.

The discovery has renewed concerns over the illegal dumping of construction waste believed to have originated from Singapore, despite previous enforcement action and assurances from Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) that no permits had been issued for construction waste exports to Malaysia.

The issue first came to light in August following reports that large quantities of construction and demolition waste had been transported into Pontian and dumped at several locations, including Kampung Sungai Karang, Kampung Sungai Senai and Kampung Simpang Kiri.

Investigations identified nine Malaysian companies allegedly linked to the transportation and dumping activities, prompting the Johor government to establish a special task force involving SWCorp, local authorities, police and the district administration.

On Aug 17, NEA informed SWCorp that Singapore would halt the export of construction and demolition waste to Malaysia. It reiterated that such waste was not permitted to be exported for disposal and reminded licensed waste management facilities to comply with regulations.

SWCorp said all construction waste must be disposed of at approved or gazetted facilities and warned that enforcement would be intensified to prevent further illegal dumping, in line with the Johor Clean City 2030 aspiration.
62b49bc7f7abf6f9: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.
How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?
—Amit Katwala
Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.
Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.
—Casey Crownhart
MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

What’s next for IVF

IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that.

Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease.
The technologies could make IVF more effective and accessible. But they’re also raising difficult ethical questions about how far reproductive medicine should go.

9cb9694735c690ed: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia must not repeat its colonial-era experience with tin mining in developing its rare earth industry, Datuk Dr Mohd Radzi Md Jidin (PN-Putrajaya) has warned.
He questioned the extent of the Science, Technology and Innovation Ministry's (Mosti) involvement in research and development (R&D) into rare earth processing.

"To this day, our country has rare earth supplies but no means, no approach and no technology to process them," he said while debating the ministry's allocation under the 2027 Budget at the Dewan Rakyat committee stage.

Radzi said growing interest from world powers in Malaysia's rare earth deposits was evident, noting that 80 per cent of the deposits were located in Terengganu, Kelantan, Perak, Kedah and Pahang, within forest reserves.
"Yesterday, the French president came to Malaysia, and one of his main aims was to discuss the supply of REE, or rare earths, from Malaysia," he said.
He also cited Malaysia's Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States, saying rare earths were among its main components.

Radzi highlighted the government's decision to allow the export of up to 100 metric tonnes of raw rare earths for R&D, subject to a commitment to establish processing facilities in Malaysia within three years.
He questioned the extent of Mosti's involvement in developing domestic processing capabilities and whether it was collaborating with local universities.
He said he did not want private companies, particularly those with predominantly foreign shareholders, to reap most of the benefits from the country's mineral resources.
Drawing parallels with the tin industry, Radzi said Malaya produced about 55 per cent of the world's tin in 1900.

"The colonialists plundered the tin. They took the benefits of tin mining back to their own countries. Some of us benefited, but what did they leave behind? All that is left to us is the mining pools.
"In the end, what is left in our country, as the Bachok MP mentioned just now, is badly affected catchment areas, badly affected water supplies and very limited benefit to Malaysia," he said.

53bf28c36494803d: The activist admits his mental state has been negatively affected by the 10-year sentence increase
Originally published on Global Voices
Joshua Wong released from Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre on June 17, 2019. HKFP's File photo.

This article was originally published by Hong Kong Free Press on November 16, 2026. The following version is edited and republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement. It is also part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” You can support this coverage by donating here.

In a letter from a Hong Kong prison earlier this year, jailed activist Joshua Wong expressed dread over the looming sentence in his foreign collusion case. “Fretting about whether it’s 2032 or 2037, my mental state is hardly all right,” he wrote in Chinese, weighing when he might regain his freedom.
The agony inevitably stems from this: What if it’s 2037? Well, it’s easy [for people] to sympathise in the moment, but it’s difficult to be consistent, and it will only get harder.

The 30-year-old pro-democracy activist has already spent almost six years behind bars over various offences and was set for release in January 2026, until authorities charged him last year with conspiring to collude with foreign forces — the second case against him under the Beijing-imposed national security law. His case is one of the most high-profile examples of changing judicial norms in Hong Kong.
A prison letter Joshua Wong wrote to friend and former fellow student activist Louis Lee in February 2026. This photo was taken on September 30, 2026. Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP. Used with permission.

On November 5, just two months before he was due to be released, a court sentenced him to 10 more years in prison for colluding with foreign forces. He is now expected to serve until late 2036, when he turns 40.

Standing in the courtroom as his new sentence was announced, Wong shook his head slightly and made notes, but appeared calm. Judge William Tam ruled that Wong’s offence was one of a “grave nature” under the national security law, which carries a minimum penalty of 10 years in jail and up to life imprisonment.
The judge knocked off three years from a 13-year starting sentence for Wong’s guilty plea.

In prison correspondence shared with HKFP by two close friends ahead of Wong’s sentencing, the former poster child of Hong Kong’s democracy movement had at times reflected on the weight of facing an additional decade behind bars. He expressed anxiety over fading from the memory of his friends — and from society at large. In one letter, Wong wrote:
I have no idea how much more I will lose in the passing of time. Responsibility is, in fact, response-ability. But who will respond? I can’t help but ponder and doubt.

Once a pro-democracy activist dedicated first and foremost to Hong Kong’s political future, Wong began campaigning as a charismatic, eloquent student leader who dared to stand up to the authorities — even to Beijing. Hong Kong is an overseas territory of China, and has increasingly been pressured to conform to China’s political goals in recent years, despite agreements that Hong Kong would retain “a high degree of autonomy” when handed over to China in 1997. A Netflix documentary about him is succinctly titled “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower.”

Yet, after years behind bars, Wong has changed. The teenager who focused single-mindedly on Hong Kong’s democracy movement has become even more caring for those around him despite being separated by prison walls, according to his friends.
Tiffany Chin, a former student activist who campaigned alongside Wong, said. The pair were once romantically involved and are now friends. She shared:
For me, it doesn’t feel like we’re the only ones supporting him. In fact, he has been supporting people on the outside in his own way.
And, with the political causes he once championed now firmly crushed, Wong has turned inward to reflect on himself. In another letter, he wrote:
We had held such high aspirations for society from a young age, we should hold ourselves to the same standard. Only by refusing a life of mediocrity can we be worthy of the world we envisioned.
From “robot” to caring friend

On a bright summer day in June 2025, while serving a sentence for subversion at Stanley Prison, Wong was arrested behind bars and brought to court the same day on a fresh charge of conspiracy to collude with foreign forces.
The prosecution came without warning. That day, Chin and Louis Lee, another longtime friend of Wong’s, rushed to the court after hearing the news, but failed to see him in person.

Authorities accused him of conspiring with Nathan Law — another high-profile, pro-democracy student activist — in 2020 to collude with foreign elements, citing Wong’s sharing of Law’s social media posts calling for international sanctions against Hong Kong as evidence.
The unexpected new charge was devastating to Wong. That month, he confessed he was under a lot of pressure — a vulnerability he rarely showed in the past, Chin said.

After so many prison terms and all the ups and downs over the last decade… he seldom openly showed vulnerability. So when he felt the need to say so bluntly that he was not OK, I truly believed he wasn’t.

Having begun campaigning at the age of 14, Wong has been in and out of prison throughout his years of activism. He now has a total of eight criminal convictions, including three separate offences linked to unlawful assembly and two national security offences.
Joshua Wong is photographed inside the Lai Chi Kwok Reception Centre on March 4, 2021. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.

Born in 1996 to a Christian family – one year before Hong Kong was handed over to China from British rule – Wong rose to prominence in 2011 when he co-founded student protest group Scholarism amid a public outcry against a proposed patriotic education curriculum.

The following year, Scholarism activists occupied the forecourt outside Hong Kong government headquarters and staged a hunger strike to protest what they described as a “brainwashing” curriculum. In a widely reported encounter, the teenager Wong twice refused to shake hands with then-city leader Leung Chun-ying, who visited the protest site alongside education officials.
Hundreds of thousands of people rallied behind Wong and his fellow student activists, forcing the government to back down and shelve the proposal.

But the teenage campaigner was also viewed as somewhat distant and domineering among the inner circle of Scholarism. Lee, who mainly handled protest logistics at that time, described his relationship with Wong as “almost like that of a boss and subordinate.”

Chin, who joined Scholarism around 2013, similarly described Wong as a deeply rational figure who seldom expressed his emotions. “Ten years ago, everyone described him as someone without many feelings,” she said. “Like a robot.”
Wong might even come across as “rude,” she added, noting that he rarely said thanks to others during that period.

A large part of Wong’s youth coincided with a period of escalating social movements in Hong Kong. Just two years after the anti-patriotic education protests, the city saw the 79-day Umbrella Movement in 2014. Wong, then aged 17, took centre stage in mobilising public support for student protesters, who demanded democratic reform and universal suffrage.

In a demonstration that sparked the Umbrella Movement, Wong and other student leaders led protesters into the forecourt of the government headquarters in an action dubbed “Reclaiming Civic Square,” seeking to escalate their campaign. That eventually resulted in Wong’s first criminal conviction.

In 2016, Wong and fellow student leaders Alex Chow and Nathan Law were found guilty of unlawful assembly. Though initially spared prison, Wong later served around 69 days behind bars – his first jail term – following a government appeal in 2017. His penalty was ultimately quashed by the Court of Final Appeal in 2018.

Scholarism disbanded in 2016. Wong and several former members, as well as young activists like Law, went on to establish Demosisto, a political party advocating for “democratic self-determination” in the city. Wong served as general secretary.
Lee and Chin did not join the new party, and they grew estranged from Wong during that period.

That year, Law was elected to the Legislative Council, making him the youngest lawmaker in Hong Kong history at the age of 23. He won over 50,000 votes, giving Demosisto a strong popular mandate. The prospect of youth democracy activism appeared bright at the time, but Law was eventually disqualified from his seat in 2017 following an oath-taking controversy.
From left: Joshua Wong, Agnes Chow, and Nathan Law, photographed on March 10, 2018. Photo via HKFP. Used with permission.
Reconnections
It was only after Wong’s detention in late 2020 that Lee and Chin reconnected with him, beginning with an exchange of letters.

In 2019, citywide protests and unrest triggered by a controversial extradition bill engulfed the city. Wong and Demosisto were heavily involved in the protests, with the activist frequently lobbying foreign governments to impose sanctions on Hong Kong officials and halt the export of crowd control equipment to the city’s police force.

Then, in June 2020, Beijing imposed the national security law, effectively crushing political dissent in the city. Demosisto disbanded on the eve of the law’s enactment, while Nathan Law left Hong Kong in self-exile.
Written by Hong Kong Free Press
d1c0f3f0d45e2a5b: United Launch Alliance (ULA) says poor booster performance appears to have doomed Sunday's Vulcan mission, which lost an Amazon Leo satellite payload on the rocket's return to flight.

ULA's initial assessment points to trouble almost immediately. "Early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance," it said. As a result, stage separation occurred at too low an altitude, and the rocket was not traveling fast enough for the payload to reach orbit.

The second stage appeared to perform well, with its RL10 engines operating as planned, but that wasn't enough to make up for the shortfall, and the mission failed. ULA lost telemetry approximately ten minutes into flight.

An investigation is underway, led by ULA and overseen by the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which had to activate two Debris Response Areas where debris was falling. The agency directs aircraft to leave these areas, and others are prevented from entering.

Late Wednesday afternoon GMT, ULA posted an update stating that it looks like it might be the fuel supply rather than the BE-4 engines that caused the underperformance of the booster. The company wrote: “Preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines."

Previous flights had been blighted by problems with the solid rocket boosters, designed to give the rocket a kick at launch. Those issues prompted a stand-down while investigators examined the cause. This time, ULA said: "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch."

Attention therefore turns to Vulcan's liquid-fueled core stage, powered by two Blue Origin BE-4 engines, though that does not establish an engine fault. Fuel delivery or another first-stage system could also be responsible, and the investigation is ongoing.

The BE-4 also powers Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which exploded on the launchpad during a ground test in May. In August, Blue Origin boss Dave Limp said that the issue originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines. Modifications were made to deal with the problem.

The upper stage's apparently normal performance may offer some reassurance to NASA, although the investigation remains at an early stage. The agency dropped the delayed Exploration Upper Stage earlier this year and is pursuing a stretched Centaur V alongside its existing interim cryogenic propulsion stage as options for Artemis IV.
NASA is targeting Artemis IV for early 2028 and Artemis V for later that year.
ULA said: "We truly understand the impact this has on our customers and are committed to returning to flight as safely and quickly as we can."

The failure also dents ULA's otherwise impressive launch record. A predecessor of Vulcan, the Atlas V, has a 100 percent success record for payloads reaching orbit. However, it uses Russian RD-180 engines, a dependency the US wishes to remove. ®
Updated at 1747 GMT to reflect ULA's statement about the likely cause of the failure.
792da3987dfe9eae: China is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit for the third time in the past 25 years. The gathering in Shenzhen will see the leaders of the US, China and Russia sit down together for a formal three-way meeting for the first time in history. But what does China want from the summit? I see it as having three main priorities. First is to consolidate its position as one of the world’s most important diplomatic hubs. Second is to set out its vision for a new global order. And third is to take advantage of favourable geopolitical conditions, primarily brought about by US setbacks in Iran and Russia’s quagmire in Ukraine, to adjust the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow. 1. A diplomatic hub Hosting national leaders and other high-level officials has become a key feature of Chinese diplomacy in recent years. President Xi Jinping has welcomed over 25 world leaders to China so far in 2026. These include Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez and the UK’s former prime minister, Keir Starmer. Beijing’s push to become a key diplomatic convener is a notable break from earlier forms of Chinese diplomacy. In the 2010s, the assertive and confrontational approach of Chinese officials on the international stage was widely known as “wolf warrior” diplomacy. The name is derived from a series of patriotic Chinese action films, also called Wolf Warrior. In this period, Chinese officials used social media to share controversial political memes and spar with foreign politicians and critical journalists, drawing condemnation in diplomatic circles. This belligerent approach was retired in the early 2020s. Notable wolf warriors such as China’s former foreign affairs minister Qin Gang and ministry spokesman Zhao Lijian were reassigned or removed from their posts. China’s hosting of the latest Apec summit is in line with Beijing’s new diplomatic strategy, suggesting it has acknowledged the limitations of the wolf warrior approach. 2. Reshaping the global order As well as showcasing China’s shifting approach to diplomacy, hosting major international events such as the Apec summit is a central part of Beijing’s wider ambitions to reshape the global order – most notably as a venue to gain greater legitimacy for its vision. This vision was summarised in a 45-page white paper released by China’s state council in June. The paper signalled the Chinese government’s desire to evolve from being a participant of the existing international system to the architect of a new global order where China and the global south play a greater role. The same message was repeated in the run-up to the Shenzhen summit. In a speech in late October, China’s foreign affairs minister Wang Yi declared that “the rise of the global south is the most momentous shift since the second world war”. He framed China’s hosting of multilateral events such as Apec as a vehicle to give developing countries a greater voice on the international stage. It is this vision that China seeks to convey to the wider world through the Shenzhen summit. 3. Great-power engagement The timing of the Shenzhen summit works in China’s favour. With the US and Russia currently bogged down in costly military conflicts in Iran and Ukraine respectively, and Trump reeling from a punishing electoral defeat, it is Xi who holds the strongest geopolitical hand. When Trump, Putin and Xi sit down together in Shenzhen on November 19, China may be in a position to push harder on the terms of its engagement with Washington and Moscow. A primary goal for China is to stabilise the global economy, which has been disrupted by the war in Iran. However, many commentators remain sceptical that the three-way meeting will deliver any concrete outcomes. The US and China recently extended their fragile trade truce, delaying the expiry date until January 2027. Preventing relations from deteriorating is thus probably in the interests of both countries. And on various other issues, the three leaders are entering the meeting with vastly different ambitions. Trump is focused primarily on agreeing a three-way nuclear arms control agreement. But China has historically refused to discuss any limitations on its nuclear arsenal while its stockpile of warheads remains smaller than the US and Russia’s. On the other hand, Russia has pushed to make Ukraine a central part of the talks. It is aiming to build support for a settlement to the war on terms favourable to Moscow. However, China has sought to keep Ukraine off the agenda entirely, fearing political backlash and deeper economic countermeasures from the EU should it back such a settlement. Regardless of this, the 2026 Apec summit offers a window into what China hopes to achieve on the international stage as well as the world it perceives itself to be in. 7f054a92225181ea: The Home Office has awarded a contract worth £178 million to a public-private hosting services joint venture - without competition - to support critical national infrastructure.

According to a notice published last week, Crown Hosting Data Centres (CHDC) won the seven-year contract to support "essential national infrastructure underpinning the Home Office's most critical systems, including border security, the Police National Computer (PNC), and core intelligence environments."

CHDC is a joint venture between the Cabinet Office, which owns 25 percent, and Ark Data Centres Ltd, which owns the rest. It was set up in 2015 for the express purpose of providing hosting services for the government.
The award was made through an existing framework agreement, set up in February 2022, awarded to CHDC without competition via a Voluntary Ex-Ante Transparency Notice.
The service is set to support Critical National Infrastructure, although the notice does not reveal specific services requested.

Mention of continued support for the Police National Computer may raise eyebrows. The Home Office is managing the transition of the aging legacy system to the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) under the National Law Enforcement Data Program (NLEDP).

A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of LEDS products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." The government had previously set a target of decommissioning the PNC in 2022.
The Register has asked the Home Office to clarify why Crown Hosting support is necessary beyond this date.
The PNC – which is based on mainframe technology dating from the 1970s – was at the center of a scandal in 2021 when a technology failure led to the loss of 413,000 records of evidence.

The incident, which left then Prime Minister Boris Johnson floundering in Parliament, was the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records to be deleted from the PNC, a system running on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe-based at a datacenter in Hendon, London.
In 2022, the Cabinet Office awarded a contract worth up to £250 million to CHDC, also without outside competition. ®

2a320e6357c66bb2: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. Tencent, which owns the developer of massively popular eSports titles including "League of Legends", has sizeable operations in other areas from cloud computing to entertainment.

03692ec60cac1bbf: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication.

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

0bbe03ed3a7069de: SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned.

Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward.
Yet DSAG, which represents SAP users in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access.

In July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he said.

However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn. It said on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway.

Henzler told The Reg: "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?'

"Now it's a completely new strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a big shift in the technology and architectures?"
The DSAG chair said the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the new Joule suite is the commercial model.

"Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he said.

"In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, independent of the commercials."

The Register asked SAP to respond to Henzler's concerns. A spokesperson said: "The offering separates a customer's commercial commitment to cloud ERP from the timing of its operational migration. Customers that meet the applicable commercial and technical requirements can use supported AI capabilities with eligible ECC or on-premises SAP S/4HANA systems while modernizing their landscape. Eligibility is not determined by the number of ERP instances and can therefore also extend to single-instance customers."

There are thousands of SAP ERP users worldwide, including some of the world's largest businesses. Despite efforts to get them onto the latest iteration – S/4HANA – and in the cloud, where the vendor promised it could gather a greater "share of wallet" from customers, there has been a dogged resistance to these complex and time-consuming migrations.

Gartner figures for Q4 2024 showed only 39 percent of worldwide ECC customers – from a total of 35,000 – had bought or subscribed to SAP S/4HANA licenses. More recently, The Reg uncovered that SAP was about €2 billion short of its target for getting customers off on-prem support.
Customers still running older ERP systems face pressure to embrace AI-supported automation. Whether SAP's terms help them do that – or simply help move them onto RISE – remains the question. ®

3bfa2d4b216e269c: SAN FRANCISCO: Scandal-hit Californian chip giant Nvidia said Tuesday it has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its "Hopper" series to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing's access to powerful US semiconductors.
Advanced Nvidia chips are the world's top hardware for training and running AI tools -- making them highly sensitive equipment in the tech race between Washington and Beijing.

Lucrative sales of Nvidia chips -- and allegations they are smuggled to China through third countries -- are in the spotlight after former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom some US officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing.
In the third quarter, "sales of licensed Hopper data centre products to China was US$2.4 billion," interim CEO Colette Kress told an earnings call Tuesday.
But "our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China."
Kress did not give a reason for the decision.
Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told AFP "the timing says quite a lot."

"We don't know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first."
This year, the Trump administration began allowing limited sales of the flagship "H200" chip from Nvidia's "Hopper" series to China.
But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also seen as reluctant to buy H200s as its homegrown chip industry gains momentum.
Washington still bans the export of Nvidia's even more advanced "Blackwell" and "Rubin" GPUs to China, citing security concerns as advanced AI has military applications.
Huang's affair with Alice Huang, a former director of a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has tanked Nvidia's market value.

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International -- a company under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese tech firms obtain Nvidia chips in violation of US export controls.
As the scandal deepens, the US moved Monday to close loopholes in those restrictions.

Its new rules aim to crack down on both chip smuggling to China and the large gray market of Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres full of high-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian countries.
Chandy Ye, a dual-qualified Hong Kong solicitor and mainland China lawyer, told AFP that the practical impact of Nvidia's decision to stop Hopper shipments to China would be limited.

"Chinese authorities have already been actively steering the domestic tech sector away from procuring H200s since January 2026, meaning the local ecosystem has long been adjusting to this decoupling," she said.

"The far more consequential development is the sweeping new interim rule from the US Commerce Department restricting remote access to advanced computing capabilities," which closes a "massive loophole."
