43c6c4ac0068ccff: JAKARTA، Nov 18 — Indonesia’s central bank has raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to six per cent، a pre-emptive move aimed at stabilising the weakening rupiah and containing inflation amid heightened global economic uncertainty. Bank Indonesia (BI) Communications Department executive director Ramdan Denny Prakoso said the decision was made at the central bank’s two-day Board of Governors meeting which concluded on Wednesday. The meeting also saw the Deposit Facility rate raised by 25 basis points to 5.25 per cent and the Lending Facility rate by the same margin to 6.75 per cent. “The increase is a measure to further strengthen rupiah exchange rate stabilisation against the impact of rising global uncertainty، as well as a pre-emptive measure to keep inflation in 2026 and 2027 within the target range of 2.5 per cent، plus or minus one percentage point، ” he said in a statement on Wednesday. The latest increase marks BI’s first benchmark rate hike since June 18، when it raised the rate to 5.75 per cent، a level maintained for the following four months through October. Ramdan said the rupiah stood at Rp18,245 (RM4.11) against the US dollar on Tuesday، weakening 0.66 per cent from its end-October level، amid persistent global uncertainty and weak foreign investor sentiment in the domestic stock market. He said the central bank would continue directing monetary policy towards strengthening rupiah exchange rate stability while maintaining accommodative macroprudential measures to support lending to the real sector and preserve financial system stability. He said BI would also optimise foreign exchange intervention through offshore non-deliverable forward transactions، as well as spot and domestic non-deliverable forward transactions in the domestic market، alongside measures to strengthen banking liquidity. “Going forward، BI projects that the rupiah exchange rate will remain stable، supported by its commitment، attractive yields، inflation controlled within the target، and favourable domestic economic prospects، ” he said. Ramdan said global financial market volatility remained elevated due to continuing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East، growing political instability in Europe and expectations of further monetary tightening in the United States. He said BI expected global economic growth to remain weak at around 3.1 per cent in 2026، with inflation remaining elevated at approximately 4.6 per cent، prompting investors to reduce portfolio investments in emerging markets. Despite external pressures، he noted that Indonesia’s economy expanded by 5.47 per cent year-on-year in the third quarter of 2026، accelerating from 5.29 per cent in the preceding quarter، supported mainly by domestic consumption and investment. He said BI projected Indonesia’s economy to grow between 4.9 and 5.7 per cent in 2026، while annual inflation eased to 3.23 per cent in October from 3.28 per cent in September، remaining within the central bank’s target range. On capital flows، Ramdan said foreign portfolio investment in Indonesia’s stock market recorded net outflows of US$900 million in the fourth quarter up to November 16، although overall capital flows registered net inflows of US$4.80 billion، supported by government global sukuk and bond issuances، as well as inflows into government securities. He said Indonesia’s foreign exchange reserves stood at US$146.8 billion at the end of October، equivalent to 5.3 months of imports، while bank lending grew 13.21 per cent year-on-year in the same month. To support financing، he said BI was preparing to introduce macroprudential liquidity incentives of up to three per cent of banks’ third-party funds from Dec 1، targeting lending to businesses that support job creation and micro، small and medium enterprises. The central bank also plans to introduce cross-currency repurchase transactions by March 2027، allowing banks to obtain rupiah liquidity using foreign currency-denominated BI securities and sukuk as collateral، he added. — Bernama

d39ad68dec251893: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.

In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.

It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation.

The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta.

All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything.
"We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP.
Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation.

"Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested."

The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers.

The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns.

MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny.

Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses.

There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

"AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear."

MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases.

Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

Abdul Rasheed also emphasised that diversification remained a key strategy guiding Malaysia’s developments across various sectors, including date centres. Therefore, the (US) restrictions are not expected to have a significant impact on data centre investments. “Based on our estimates of ongoing and planned projects, investment momentum in data centres is expected to remain strong at least until 2028,” he said, adding that sustained underlying demand for data centres would also create lasting economic linkages for Malaysia. According to Abdul Rasheed, the positive fundamentals are also consistent with the Malaysian Investment Development Authority’s (MIDA) approved information, communication and technology (ICT) investments, which increased to about RM38.9 billion in the first quarter of this year. **Impact of US midterm elections** Commenting on the US midterm election results, which could see the Democrats take control of Congress in January and increase scrutiny of the Trump administration’s tariff, data centre and AI policies, he said it was still too early to assess the potential implications for Malaysia’s economy as the situation continued to evolve. He stressed that strengthening the country’s economic fundamentals and foundations would help shield Malaysia from global developments and uncertainties. “On our part, we will continue to monitor the situation closely and assess its potential impact on the economy and financial markets, as well as the measures that we can put in place. “In addition, this is where buffers matter. That is why I always stress the importance of building up buffers during good times, when we are (in a) strong (position), so that we can always draw on them during difficult periods or in the event of unexpected developments,” he added. — Bernama
b5b42c8fd0be99c1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — The implementation of targeted fuel subsidies has not resulted in a significant increase in the prices of essential goods or public transport fares, based on monitoring by the Ministry of Domestic Trade and Cost of Living (KPDN). According to the ministry, the distribution of subsidies through the Subsidised Diesel Control System (SKDS) and Subsidised Petrol Control System (SKPS) took into account their potential impact on the transportation costs of essential goods, land public transport fares, as well as ferry and passenger boat services. “Based on monitoring of essential goods prices and public transport fares, no significant price increases have been reported following the implementation of targeted fuel subsidies, which began on June 10, 2024, for SKDS and September 30, 2025, for SKPS,” the ministry said in a written reply published on the official Parliament website. The reply was in response to a question from Datuk Awang Hashim (PN-Pendang), who sought an assessment of the effectiveness of targeted fuel subsidies in addressing the operating costs of goods transportation and their impact on consumer prices. He also asked about the intervention mechanisms that would be implemented should the government’s fiscal savings from the subsidies lead to higher prices for consumers. KPDN said more than 850 Price Monitoring Officers (PPH) were deployed daily to collect price data from over 2,000 business premises nationwide. The data was analysed to detect unreasonable price fluctuations and serve as an early warning mechanism. The ministry added that price information was also made available to consumers through the PriceCatcher application, enabling them to monitor prevailing market prices and make informed purchasing decisions. It said targeted fuel subsidies for the transport sector also served as a government intervention to curb leakages and misappropriations, while mitigating the impact of rising transportation costs on the prices of goods. KPDN said enforcement efforts had also been intensified to curb price manipulation and profiteering under the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering Act 2011 (Act 723). These include stepped-up monitoring and inspections to ensure that targeted fuel subsidies are not used as a pretext to increase the prices of goods, while safeguarding consumer interests. As part of its intervention measures, the ministry conducts a series of operations known as Ops Kesan whenever policy changes or economic developments could potentially affect the prices of goods and services. “Up to 2026, six series of Ops Kesan have been conducted, including Ops Kesan 2.0 following the implementation of targeted diesel subsidies and Ops Kesan 6.0 to address the risk of profiteering arising from global cost pressures. “Through these operations, KPDN monitors the entire supply chain and is empowered to issue written notices under Section 21 of Act 723 to examine changes in costs and profit margins. Legal action may be taken against parties found to have engaged in profiteering,” the ministry said. — Bernama
5f652bed411805f9: NOVEMBER 18 — Your next smartphone, cup of coffee or pair of sneakers may have travelled thousands of kilometres and passed through several countries before reaching you. That journey is becoming a growing headache for businesses. From trade wars and supply disruptions to rising fuel costs and carbon regulations, the global supply chains companies once took for granted are under pressure. And going green is increasingly becoming a matter of commercial survival, not environmental goodwill. The problem is that corporate promises have yet to translate into meaningful action. A recent MIT survey found that 83% of companies consider sustainability critical to their long-term success. Yet 68% admitted that tariff uncertainty had forced them to delay or abandon sustainability plans. Nearly a third said the disruptions had actually increased their emissions. In other words, sustainability is still one of the first casualties when business gets tough. That could prove costly. Research by FedEx found that 81% of consumers in Asia-Pacific prefer buying from companies that appear to operate sustainably, while nearly 40% are willing to pay more for environmentally friendly packaging. In Southeast Asia, more than half of small and medium businesses now factor sustainability into their supply chain decisions. Businesses may be tempted to put environmental commitments on hold when costs rise, but customers are not necessarily putting their expectations on hold with them. There is another misconception holding companies back: the idea that resilience and sustainability are competing priorities. They are not. Consider a company that depends on a single factory in one country and one type of fuel. A geopolitical crisis, sudden fuel price increase or new carbon tax could leave its entire operation exposed. Now consider a company with production spread across several regions, multiple suppliers and shorter transport routes. It is better positioned to withstand disruptions while reducing its environmental footprint. The same decisions can deliver two benefits: a more resilient business and a more sustainable supply chain. The World Economic Forum has declared the old “just-in-time” model dead. Companies that recognise this are already rethinking how their supply networks operate. Those that do not risk being caught off guard while continuing to squeeze suppliers for marginal cost savings. But rebuilding supply chains does not necessarily mean investing immediately in expensive new technology. Green logistics discussions often gravitate towards futuristic solutions such as hydrogen-powered trucks, electric ships and sustainable aviation fuel. These technologies matter, but businesses could be overlooking more immediate opportunities to cut emissions. MIT found that only 8% of freight fleets have fully switched to low-emission energy. Most still run on diesel. Waiting for every truck to become electric before making progress is unrealistic. There are ways to make existing fleets cleaner without replacing a single vehicle. Better route planning, consolidated loads and real-time tracking can help reduce unnecessary journeys and fuel consumption. The first priority should be knowing where emissions are coming from. Companies need systems that measure their carbon footprint across their entire supply chains, including emissions generated by suppliers. These typically account for more than 80% of a company's total footprint. Without that information, businesses are effectively trying to manage a problem they cannot see. Artificial intelligence can then help optimise delivery routes, cargo loads and warehouse energy consumption. FedEx, for instance, has developed tools that allow customers to see the carbon cost of individual shipments in real time. Technology, however, cannot compensate for a company that treats sustainability as somebody else's responsibility. MIT found that 57% of companies with dedicated cross-functional sustainability teams had integrated sustainability into their daily decisions. The figure fell to just 13% when responsibility was left to a single department. That gap points to a structural problem. Sustainability teams are often excluded from decisions that have the greatest long-term environmental consequences, such as where to build warehouses, which suppliers to engage for long-term contracts and how to design distribution networks. These decisions can lock in emissions for years. Yet only 33% of companies have board-level oversight of sustainability. When a crisis hits, there may be nobody senior enough to prevent environmental commitments from being sacrificed for short-term savings. Three things every business leader should know First, the winners will not necessarily be companies with the grandest sustainability pledges. They will be those that can demonstrate measurable progress and maintain it over time. Regulators increasingly want hard data, not glossy reports. Second, resilience and sustainability should not be treated as competing budget items. Regionalising production, diversifying suppliers and investing in digital planning tools can strengthen supply chains while reducing their environmental impact. Third, businesses need to be realistic about technology. Measure emissions first, make existing operations more efficient and only then consider replacing equipment. Buying expensive new technology without understanding where the biggest problems lie is unlikely to deliver the best returns. Ultimately, sustainability is no longer an optional extra that companies can showcase in their annual reports when business is doing well. Carbon has a price. Customers have expectations. Regulators are tightening scrutiny. And competitors are already finding ways to turn more sustainable operations into a commercial advantage. Companies that continue treating sustainability as a public relations exercise risk losing ground to those that recognise its value to their bottom line. The question is no longer whether businesses can afford to make their supply chains greener. It is whether they can afford not to. * The author is affiliated with the Tan Sri Omar Centre for STI Policy Studies at UCSI University and is an Adjunct Professor at the Ungku Aziz Centre for Development Studies, Universiti Malaya. He can be reached at ahmadibrahim@ucsiuniversity.edu.my. ** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
a8b50b5a87620c2c: JAKARTA: Indonesia's central bank announced a surprise interest rate hike Wednesday to bolster the rupiah as it sits around record lows against the dollar.

Bank Indonesia governor Destry Damayanti said the decision to lift borrowing costs 25 basis points to 6% was a "pre-emptive" measure to maintain inflation within policymakers' target range of 2.5-3.5%. Inflation is currently sitting at 3.2%.
"This increase is a step to further strengthen the stabilisation of the rupiah exchange rate from the impact of increasing global uncertainty," she told reporters in Jakarta.
The rupiah is Asia's worst-performing currency this year, and last week it hit 18,200 to the greenback, its weakest level on record.

The rate hike marked a "hawkish" turn by the central bank, wrote Bank Danamon Indonesia economist Irman Faiz in a note, with resilient domestic growth giving officials room for further monetary tightening.
"We expect another 25 basis-point hike in December to 6.25%, followed by a hold through 2027," he added.
"Markets pricing in a higher Fed rate path can keep US yields and the dollar elevated, adding to rupiah pressure."
Capital Economics said it expected two more 25-point hikes "given our view that further falls in the rupiah lie in store over the next twelve months".
"Failure to deliver would raise renewed concerns about the central bank’s credibility," it said.
98ba8d33554c9e5f: SHENZHEN, Nov 18 — US President Donald Trump arrived in China today, a day ahead of a historic trilateral summit with the leaders of China and Russia. Trump has said that the talks tomorrow with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen would cover the wars in Iran and Ukraine as well as nuclear disarmament. — AFP
59f2f0844142872d: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — The Madani government’s proactive measures to safeguard economic stability and ensure fuel supply amid the West Asia crisis have helped Malaysia maintain strong economic growth despite external uncertainties, said Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim. He emphasised that the government’s decisive action in addressing the West Asia crisis, supported by reforms implemented under the Madani Economy framework, has strengthened the country’s economic resilience. “As a result, Malaysia has recorded one of the region’s strongest economic performances despite the various challenges facing the world,” said Anwar in a statement issued by the Ministry of Finance today. He said the Madani government remained optimistic about the country’s economic prospects but stayed cautious about geopolitical tensions and climate-related risks weighing on the global economy as Malaysia heads into 2027. Earlier, Bank Negara Malaysia announced that the country’s economy grew 5.5 per cent in the third quarter of 2026 (3Q 2026), bringing growth in the first nine months of the year to 5.6 per cent, up from 4.8 per cent in the same period last year. Broad-based growth was supported by resilient domestic demand, which expanded by 4.8 per cent. In September 2026, Malaysia recorded its highest monthly export value on record at RM215.1 billion, surpassing the RM200 billion mark for the first time. Anwar said the government would build on previous Madani Budgets by raising the ceiling through stronger economic growth, higher investment and infrastructure development, while maintaining fiscal discipline. “However, these achievements would mean little if we neglected efforts to raise the floor for the well-being of the wider population. “Through Budget 2027, the Madani government is strengthening assistance, reducing individual income tax rates for eligible groups and improving public services,” he said. — Bernama
61ee480c5f38c2a7: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has proposed that the concession for government vehicle supply be extended to other companies — categorised by vehicle type — to break the current monopoly held by a single concessionaire. PAC chairperson Datuk Wira Mas Ermieyati Samsudin said the categories that could be opened to other companies include vans, buses, four-wheel-drive vehicles, ambulances, and motorcycles. This was one of three additional recommendations by the PAC to improve the management of government concession vehicles, following the tabling of PAC’s Follow-Up Action Report on the Management of Government Vehicles under Concession Agreements in the Dewan Rakyat today. Mas Ermieyati added that the government must also finalise and enforce a supplementary agreement with Spanco Sdn Bhd to reduce vehicle leasing costs, as well as the excessive maintenance costs incurred when vehicles remain in use beyond their lease period. She noted that the PAC’s investigation into the management of government vehicles — under a 15-year concession agreement 2 between the Finance Ministry (MOF) and Spanco — revealed weaknesses in contract management and governance practices. This has led to delays in replacing vehicles that had reached the end of their lease terms. “The delay resulted in the government incurring additional costs for leasing and maintenance, while the imposition and collection of penalties for the delayed supply of vehicles were also slow. “Overall, the PAC is satisfied with the follow-up actions taken by MOF in implementing the recommendations outlined by the PAC,” she said in a statement today. The follow-up action report outlines MOF’s responses, along with PAC’s comments, regarding the actions taken on five key recommendations from the original report presented on July 9. The PAC also proposed expanding the supply concession to include vehicles intended for critical and rugged use — such as ambulances — to ensure that essential vehicles remain consistently available and can be replaced promptly in the event of a breakdown or accident. “The PAC further suggested that the government explore the adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) to reduce reliance on fossil fuels, drive the development of the nation’s green technology industry, and attract foreign investment in this sector. This will support the national goal of becoming carbon-neutral by 2050. “Furthermore, the PAC recommends continuous training for officers who manage vehicles within ministries and departments. It also calls on the government to prioritise data security and integrity when implementing the online system designed to manage and monitor concession vehicles,” she said. The PAC has also requested the government to ensure the system is fully accessible and functional in rural and remote areas, including in Sabah and Sarawak, Mas Ermieyati added. She said the PAC will continue to monitor the implementation of follow-up actions to ensure that the management of public funds adheres to the principles of transparency, accountability, and the best value for the people’s money. — Bernama
ad7ac4ab92a0752a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 18 — Scandal-hit Californian chip giant Nvidia said yesterday it has stopped shipping artificial intelligence chips from its “Hopper” series to China, as scrutiny grows over Beijing’s access to powerful US semiconductors. Advanced Nvidia chips are the world’s top hardware for training and running AI tools — making them highly sensitive equipment in the tech race between Washington and Beijing. Lucrative sales of Nvidia chips — and allegations they are smuggled to China through third countries — are in the spotlight after former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman whom some US officials reportedly suspect of spying for Beijing. In the third quarter, “sales of licensed Hopper data centre products to China was $2.4 billion,” interim CEO Colette Kress told an earnings call Tuesday. But “our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China.” Kress did not give a reason for the decision. Dilin Wu, a research strategist at Pepperstone, told AFP “the timing says quite a lot.” “We don’t know exactly what prompted the decision to stop shipments, but it certainly looks like Nvidia is trying to draw a clearer line around its China business and reassure regulators that compliance comes first.” This year, the Trump administration began allowing limited sales of the flagship “H200” chip from Nvidia’s “Hopper” series to China. But US conditions have made it difficult for shipments to be approved, with Beijing also seen as reluctant to buy H200s as its homegrown chip industry gains momentum. Washington still bans the export of Nvidia’s even more advanced “Blackwell” and “Rubin” GPUs to China, citing security concerns as advanced AI has military applications. Huang’s affair with Alice Huang, a former director of a Singapore-based cloud computing company, has tanked Nvidia’s market value. Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, previously led Megaspeed International — a company under investigation for allegedly helping Chinese tech firms obtain Nvidia chips in violation of US export controls. As the scandal deepens, the United States moved Monday to close loopholes in those restrictions. Its new rules aim to crack down on both chip smuggling to China and the large gray market of Chinese companies renting computing power from data centres full of high-end Nvidia chips in Southeast Asian countries. Chandy Ye, a dual-qualified Hong Kong solicitor and mainland China lawyer, told AFP that the practical impact of Nvidia’s decision to stop Hopper shipments to China would be limited. “Chinese authorities have already been actively steering the domestic tech sector away from procuring H200s since January 2026, meaning the local ecosystem has long been adjusting to this decoupling,” she said. “The far more consequential development is the sweeping new interim rule from the US Commerce Department restricting remote access to advanced computing capabilities,” which closes a “massive loophole.” — AFP
ebd5c0142e45ba60: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Umno has condemned the circulation of purported Federal Territories Pardons Board minutes concerning Datuk Seri Najib Razak's conditional pardon, denouncing the leak as a deliberate “provocation” to undermine the royal prerogative and demanding that Putrajaya clarify whether the Yang di-Pertuan Agong gave royal consent for their disclosure. In a statement today, Umno secretary-general Datuk Seri Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki said the party viewed the dissemination of the confidential records with “deep regret” and treated the matter “seriously”. He directed pointed criticism at former DAP lawmaker Tony Pua, who uploaded screenshots of the purported board minutes onto his personal Facebook account. Asyraf stressed that the sovereign authority to remit, suspend, or commute criminal sentences remains the exclusive prerogative of the King under Article 42(1) of the Federal Constitution, insisting that all documentation originating from Pardons Board proceedings must be treated with utmost “care, confidentiality and respect”. “The main question that needs to be answered is whether the declassification and dissemination of the minutes had the consent of His Majesty the Yang di-Pertuan Agong,” the statement said. While acknowledging that the federal government is reviewing the declassification of the documents, Asyraf argued that any public disclosure directly touching upon proceedings presided over by the King requires prior royal assent. He characterized the leak as “a form of insult and provocation” orchestrated to trigger partisan debate that demeans the monarch, accusing Pua of seeking to “appears to continually exploit” the sensitive clemency process “as political fodder” with disregard for the constitutional monarchy. Demanding immediate transparency from the federal administration, Umno urged Putrajaya to detail the statutory basis of any declassification, identify which authority sanctioned the disclosure, and confirm whether the palace was formally consulted. Asyraf warned that if official protocols or secrecy laws were breached, enforcement agencies must take unyielding action to safeguard the sovereignty of the Malay Rulers and constitutional conventions. The Umno statement conspicuously avoided addressing the substantive contents of the leaked document, which revealed that Attorney General Tan Sri Mohd Dusuki Mokhtar and Federal Territories Minister Hannah Yeoh formally opposed granting Najib a conditional pardon during the Sept 18 meeting. The unverified minutes also recorded that the King was “inclined” to grant clemency, allowing the former prime minister to complete his custodial sentence at his residence after settling an RM50 million fine. The political controversy erupts just days after Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail informed Parliament on Nov 12 that he would seek Cabinet approval to formally declassify the records, with Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil noting that ministers had requested legal counsel from the attorney-general. The episode marks renewed friction over Pua's social media commentary on Najib's clemency, following a police probe in early 2024 when federal investigators summoned the former parliamentarian over posts criticising the initial royal reduction of Najib's sentence and fine.
59e981982b811a74: TEHRAN, Nov 18 — Iran’s army chief Amir Hatami said today that Tehran’s response to any new attacks by the United States would be “more devastating” and directed at both US forces and their allies. “Should the enemy make a mistake and repeat actions that have previously led them to despair, our response — directed at both the enemy and their backers — will undoubtedly be even more devastating and will know no geographical boundaries,” Hatami said, according to Iran’s Fars news agency. — AFP
2b26bcf63bd61e2b: MANILA, Nov 18 — Singapore is ready to facilitate US government inspections of AI chip use in the city-state, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said, responding to concerns over alleged abuse of advanced tech in overseas data centres. In the fallout from a spy scandal at industry giant Nvidia, Washington has introduced stricter rules on exports as questions emerged over whether Singapore-based Megaspeed aided Chinese firms in accessing advanced artificial intelligence chips. “If the US has concerns about how these chips in Singapore are being used, as we have said before, we can facilitate checks by the US government,” Wong said late Tuesday. “We are not here to implement or enforce the export controls of other countries,” Wong said following a regional summit in the Philippines also attended by US President Donald Trump. “We want to make sure that businesses operating in Singapore comply with the rule of law and also comply with the export controls that other countries may have imposed,” he said. Wong said Singapore was studying the new measures announced by Washington, aimed at stopping Chinese firms from renting AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere. Data centres anywhere in the world will now need a US licence to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China or other countries under US arms embargoes. The rule also requires licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, which the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion”. Wong acknowledged that chips were being transhipped through Singapore, but warned firms against violating laws. “If there are businesses that want to make use of Singapore to circumvent these controls, or if there were businesses that were to infringe or to break Singapore laws, then obviously we will take clear and firm action,” the CNA news agency quoted him as saying. — AFP
5ceffd59edda16a3: I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology.
A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.

To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements.

Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do.
That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes.

Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages.
I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done.

But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements.

If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity.
Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®
d9dd39f488a082d0: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Proton’s Tanjong Malim plant rolled out over 23,000 vehicles last month. The national automaker said that October 2026’s figure was the company’s highest monthly production output in 24 years. The company noted that hitting this figure reflects its plant’s growing operational efficiency and capability to support a diverse product portfolio while keeping up with evolving market demand. The surge in manufacturing volume was driven by continuous nationwide orders for its newest models. Proton has previously said its October 2026 sales figure was 21,624 units, which was the second-highest for 2026. According to the National Open Data Portal, four Proton models have made their way into the 2026 year-to-date (YTD) top 10 list, including Saga, S70, e.MAS 5, and X50. We also previously reported that one in every five new Protons sold in 2026 is a Proton e.MAS. The e.MAS family has secured 3,763 deliveries in October, bringing its cumulative year-to-date (YTD) sales to 35,730 units. With two more months until the year wraps up, Proton is still not done yet. The company is currently getting ready to launch the Proton S70 RS while many are also eagerly waiting for Proton AMA02 – fondly known by most as the Saga Cross or X30. Proton surpasses 10,000 export units this year Alongside its domestic manufacturing record, Proton also revealed that it has officially crossed the 10,000-unit mark for exports. With this achievement, the national carmaker says its overseas sales are now on track to more than double in volume compared to 2025. Proton added that the export milestone underscores its expanding international footprint and reinforces its growing role as a production hub for Geely vehicles. While the company did not disclose specific models or export destinations, Geely-branded models currently assembled at Tanjong Malim for overseas markets that we are aware of include the Coolray (X50), Emgrand (S70), Okavango (X90), and EX2 (e.MAS 5). Furthermore, the Saga MC3 is expected to join the list soon, as the entry-level sedan will be released under the Geely brand in the Philippines. — SoyaCincau
78a4c87ca88edc6d: MANILA: President Donald Trump said on Wednesday the US had concluded a "very big trade deal" with the Philippines, but offered no details, while Manila said the two countries had reached only an understanding on economic cooperation.

"We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we've ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries," Trump told a state lunch event at the Philippine presidential palace.
"We were very happy with that, and we didn't know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it's a magnificent deal for both."
The Philippine president's office later said both sides reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation, but made no mention of a trade deal.
Trade representatives of both countries will work closely to translate the commitments into concrete initiatives, it said in a statement.
The deal with the Philippines would be great for US farmers and those in the energy business, Trump added on Truth Social, but gave no further details.
Negotiations on a trade deal between the two allies were not mentioned in any schedules released by either country.
There was no immediate comment from the office of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr about the deal Trump was referring to.
"The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements," said Jose Manuel Romualdez, the Philippines' ambassador to the US.
Asked whether anything was signed, Romualdez said in a text message, "None".
On Tuesday, Trump said Thailand would scrap all tariffs and substantial non-tariff barriers on its imports from the US in a trade deal expected to be finalised in coming weeks.
d0d7200cca387764: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 18 — Malaysia’s economy grew by 5.5 per cent in the third quarter (3Q) of 2026 against 5.3 per cent in the same quarter of 2025, driven by continued household spending, higher investment activity and stronger exports, said Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM). The central bank said export growth strengthened further, driven by technology-related exports across both electrical and electronics (E&E) and non-E&E products. “On the domestic front, household spending was supported by favourable labour market conditions and steady income growth. “Nevertheless, the growth moderated, reflecting a base effect from higher cash transfers in the third quarter of 2025,” it said in a statement today. BNM said the current account balance stood at RM5.7 billion in 3Q 2026, while foreign direct investment was higher at RM14.3 billion, thanks to higher reinvested earnings. On the demand side, private consumption rose 4.3 per cent year-on-year in 3Q 2026, private investment (9.4 per cent), and public investment (3.0 per cent), while net exports grew 5.7 per cent, it said. On the supply side, BNM said services recorded 5.8 per cent growth in 3Q 2026, manufacturing (7.7 per cent), construction (5.9 per cent), and agriculture (1.4 per cent), while mining declined by 6.1 per cent. Headline inflation remained stable at 1.9 per cent in 3Q 2026, while core inflation moderated further to 1.7 per cent. For the nine-month period, gross domestic product (GDP) recorded a strong growth of 5.6 per cent amid robust export performance and resilient domestic demand. Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said the Malaysian economy is therefore expected to register above 5.0 per cent growth in 2026. “Looking ahead, the economy is poised to enter 2027 from a position of strength, supported by sound fundamentals and positive economic prospects,” he said. BNM expects the GDP to grow between 4.2 per cent and 5.2 per cent in 2027. It said Malaysia’s strong initial conditions, sound fundamentals, policy measures and business dynamism will continue to buffer the economy against external shocks. Abdul Rasheed said export growth would be driven by continued global demand for technology-related products and key commodities, as well as support from travel and information, communication and technology (ICT) services. “On the domestic front, expansion in investment activity would be underpinned by the progress of multi-year projects in both the private and public sectors and the continued realisation of approved investments. “Meanwhile, household spending would benefit from favourable labour market conditions, steady income growth as well as policy measures under Budget 2027,” he said. Headline and core inflation are expected to remain moderate for the remainder of 2026, with headline inflation projected to average between 1.5 per cent and 2.5 per cent for the year, in line with earlier expectations, the central bank said. BNM said headline inflation might rise gradually towards the year-end, partly reflecting the delayed pass-through of higher input costs. “Nevertheless, targeted fuel subsidies and stable domestic demand conditions are expected to mitigate the overall impact,” it said. For 2027, it said inflation is expected to be firmer in the early part of the year, reflecting carry-over effects and delayed cost pass-through. Overall, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained, supported by stable domestic demand conditions, BNM added. — Bernama
ca4608bd11561f75: PETALING JAYA, Nov 18 — Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Seri Ismail Lasim is scheduled to seek a fresh audience with Yang di-Pertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir this Friday to map out the state assembly calendar and explore solutions for 10 sacked executive council members. A source said that the high-stakes consultation will mark their second royal engagement this week, following an audience granted yesterday at Istana Hinggap after Barisan Nasional (BN) publicly claimed that the Juasseh assemblyman had tendered his resignation, FMT reported. “He will continue performing his duties as menteri besar as usual,” the source said, adding that Ismail and Tuanku Muhriz are expected to examine the potential reappointment of the 10 dismissed councillors to restore executive functionality and ensure the state administration can govern effectively. “We hope that all parties would keep calm and pray for the best,” the source added. The upcoming palace meeting follows an administrative standoff triggered on Monday when BN announced Ismail’s resignation as menteri besar. 61df821019c60e9d: NOVEMBER 18 — Have you ever walked into a room and forgotten why you went there? Or searched frantically for your phone, only to discover it was already in your hand? For many mothers, such moments are all too familiar. Society has even given them a name: “mum brain”. The expression is often used jokingly to describe the forgetfulness, mental fog and difficulty concentrating that some women experience during pregnancy and after childbirth. But what if motherhood is not simply making women more forgetful? What if the maternal brain is undergoing an extraordinary process of adaptation? Scientists are increasingly exploring this possibility, offering a different perspective on what happens to a woman’s brain when she becomes a mother. Motherhood is a major brain transition Researchers describe the psychological, physical and neurological transition into motherhood as matrescence. Much like adolescence, when the brain undergoes significant changes in preparation for adulthood, matrescence involves adaptations that help women navigate the demands of motherhood. A scientific review published in Trends in Cognitive Sciences in 2023 by Edwina Orchard and colleagues highlighted motherhood as an important period of brain development, with possible implications extending into later life. Consider the daily responsibilities of caring for a newborn. A mother must recognise different cries, remember feeding schedules, monitor her baby’s health, respond to emotional signals and make countless decisions, often while surviving on interrupted sleep. Her brain is constantly processing information, adjusting priorities and responding to unfamiliar situations. Rather than viewing every moment of forgetfulness as evidence of declining mental ability, researchers suggest we should recognise the enormous cognitive demands associated with motherhood. Is ‘mum brain’ really a decline in intelligence? Research suggests that pregnancy may be associated with small changes in certain aspects of memory. However, cognitive performance generally remains within normal limits. Interestingly, although many mothers report forgetfulness after childbirth, studies often find little corresponding impairment in formal cognitive assessments. This does not mean their experiences are imaginary. Sleep deprivation, emotional stress, hormonal changes and the continuous responsibility of caring for a child can affect concentration and everyday memory. A mother who forgets where she placed her keys may not have a less capable brain. She may simply be managing more responsibilities than her mind can comfortably accommodate. Importantly, these changes should never be interpreted as evidence that mothers are less intelligent or less capable professionally. Could motherhood benefit the ageing brain? One intriguing area of research concerns the possible long-term effects of motherhood on brain health. Scientists are investigating whether the complex mental and emotional demands of parenting may contribute to what is known as cognitive reserve. Cognitive reserve refers to the brain’s ability to maintain functioning despite ageing or neurological changes. Imagine a city with several alternative roads. When one route becomes blocked, traffic can continue through another. Similarly, a brain with greater cognitive reserve may be better equipped to compensate for certain age-related changes. Some studies have reported associations between motherhood and favourable patterns of cognitive functioning or brain structure later in life. However, these findings remain preliminary and sometimes inconsistent. Motherhood has not been proven to prevent dementia, and having more children does not necessarily produce better cognitive health. Nevertheless, this emerging research challenges the outdated assumption that motherhood only places limitations on women’s mental abilities. What Malaysian traditions can teach us In Malaysia, the importance of supporting mothers after childbirth has long been recognised through traditional confinement practices, commonly known as pantang. Across different communities, these practices often emphasise rest, recovery, nutritious meals and assistance from family members. Although certain traditional treatments lack strong scientific evidence, the underlying principle of allowing mothers time to recover deserves attention. Research examining traditional postnatal care has highlighted the importance of family support, companionship and opportunities for rest, while also recognising that restrictive practices can sometimes create additional stress. Modern science has not established that confinement improves maternal brain development. However, the emphasis on practical assistance offers a valuable lesson: mothers should not be expected to manage every responsibility alone. Supporting mothers means supporting their brains Too often, society celebrates mothers for their ability to multitask while overlooking the physical and emotional exhaustion behind that achievement. If motherhood encourages brain adaptation, it does not mean mothers should be burdened with even more responsibilities. Partners must share childcare and household duties. Employers should provide family-friendly working arrangements, while healthcare professionals should take concerns about memory, sleep and emotional wellbeing seriously. Above all, mothers need understanding rather than criticism. The next time a mother forgets something, perhaps we should reconsider the familiar joke about “mum brain”. She may be exhausted, overwhelmed or adjusting to one of life’s most demanding transitions. For generations, scientists have studied how mothers shape their children’s developing brains. Perhaps it is time we paid equal attention to how motherhood shapes the brains of mothers themselves. Motherhood does not simply change a woman’s life. It may also reshape how her brain adapts to the world. * Dr. Nor Shuhada Murad @ Mansor author is a Senior Lecturer and Cognitive Psychology Researcher at the Tun Abdullah Ahmad Badawi Cancer Centre (PKTAAB). ** This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
17c2e30e15d669a6: SINGAPORE: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, plans to expand into five Asian markets next year with South and Southeast Asia as key priorities, its regional business head said, not long after the firm was hit with a record US$6.3 billion digital heist last month.

"We have ongoing conversations with at least five or six markets ... three of which are in quite mature stages," SB Seker told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore FinTech Festival on Wednesday. "The others are ongoing conversations."

He did not specify the new markets that Binance, which currently has operating licences in more than 10 jurisdictions, was looking at, but said details of the planned expansion were expected to be rolled out in the first quarter of next year.
Binance's expansion plans come on the heels of a security breach linked to North Korea that resulted in US$6.3 billion being stolen from its platform last month.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Binance have said North Korea was responsible for the hack, but Pyongyang has denied that.

The company, which resumed withdrawals in phases earlier this month after covering 95% of the lost tokens, said last weekend it aimed to reopen withdrawals for all remaining networks and assets by the end of this week.
The Binance heist, which has been described by experts as the largest crypto theft ever, has renewed scrutiny of inconsistent security practices in the industry.

Seker, the firm's head of APAC, said Binance contacted a number of regulators, including those in Japan, South Korea, Australia, Thailand and New Zealand, within the first 36 to 48 hours of the incident, to address questions about the scale of its impact and how the attack unfolded.
"Think of all the financial services regulators and markets where we are present," he said, adding that there was no one country that led the charge in the investigations.
Binance says the Abu Dhabi Global Market's Financial Services Regulatory Authority is its primary regulator.
Seker said that while discussions with regulators were ongoing, the conversation had moved beyond the heist to broader concerns about security threats facing the crypto industry.

"The conversations now are 'well, this is an omnipresent and spectrum-wide threat, and how does an entire ecosystem prepare for this?' It's moved away from the original incident to a much broader conversation," he said.
"We are part of the conversation, but we are not driving the conversation in isolation anymore."

7933e682ad2b584d: LONDON: British annual inflation rose to a one-year high of 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, official figures showed on Wednesday, after the Bank of England raised interest rates earlier this month for the first time in three years.

The increase was in line with economists' median prediction in a Reuters poll, while the BoE earlier this month forecast 3.7% and sees nearly 5% inflation in the second quarter of 2027 due to higher energy prices caused by the Iran war.

The BoE was the slowest major advanced central bank to raise interest rates in response to the Iran war, having initially judged that cancelling previous plans to cut rates this year would be sufficient to keep inflation in check.

But now financial markets see a 90% chance that it will raise rates again in December and price in two or three more rate hikes for 2027 – a prospect which the BoE's chief economist, Huw Pill, described last week as "not outrageous".
Core consumer price inflation – which excludes volatile energy, food, alcohol and tobacco prices – held at 2.8% as economists had expected.
The services component of CPI – which some policymakers view as a better underlying gauge of price trends – also held at an unchanged rate of 3.7%, below the Reuters poll forecast of a rise to 3.8%.
Sterling fell slightly after the data.

Britain is highly exposed to the cost of imported natural gas for heating and electricity, and regulation which delays the impact of price rises on household bills means British inflation tends to be later to rise and fall than elsewhere.

BoE governor Andrew Bailey said a drop in international energy prices at the start of the month had largely come too late to stop a roughly 20% rise in regulated household energy bills due to take effect in January.

So far there have been few signs of the BoE's biggest fear, "second-round" effects, where wages and non-energy prices increase as workers and businesses try to offset losses caused by higher energy prices.
But when they voted to raise rates, BoE officials judged this was probably just a matter of time given how long oil prices have spent at or above US$100 a barrel.
e2577fdfd894b330: HONG KONG, Nov 18 — Asian equities were mixed today as blockbuster earnings from Nvidia, which soothed concerns about the AI boom, were offset by concerns about a spy scandal that has engulfed the chip titan and shaken global markets. The tech sector — already hit by questions about profitability — has been strafed over the past week by claims that boss Jensen Huang had had a number of affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy who might have funnelled restricted chips to Beijing. The scandal forced Huang to step down on Thursday and has fanned worries about the chip titan, which is at the centre of a buildout that has helped propel world markets to record highs and boosted economic growth. In a highly anticipated earnings release Tuesday, the firm said third-quarter revenue topped expectations and doubled to more than $115 billion while net profit hit US$65.3 billion (RM269 billion). The firm also increased its forecast for next year’s revenue, predicting 75 percent growth, compared with a previous forecast of 70 percent. The figures suggested the artificial intelligence boom remained on track despite concerns that the vast sums pumped into the sector might not see returns any time soon, if at all. In a bid to reassure investors, interim CEO Colette Kress said it was “business as usual” at the firm, even after the loss of Huang, a pivotal player in the eye-watering explosion in the AI industry. The news sent Nvidia’s shares surging nearly five percent in after-hours US trade, while Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were also sharply higher. Asian markets diverged as investors weighed the earnings with concerns about the scandal. Adding to the nervousness was news that the United States moved to tighten restrictions on Chinese access to chips, while Huang has agreed to meet US lawmakers on December 1 to answer questions about chips and national security concerns. Seoul ended the day up two percent as chip giants SK hynix and Samsung enjoyed big gains, though they are still well down for the week. Tokyo also advanced, with Advantest and tech investment giant SoftBank leading the way, while Taipei was lifted by an uptick in TSMC. Shanghai, Bangkok and Jakarta also rose. However, Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Manila and Mumbai all fell. There are “still lots of unknowns for the stock that create the overhangs that investors are worried about. But the earnings show it’s still in very good shape”, wrote Neil Wilson at Saxo Markets. And SPI Asset Management’s Stephen Innes added: “The investigations and allegations aren’t findings of wrongdoing, but they certainly aren’t the backdrop Nvidia would have chosen for its earnings presentation. “Interim CEO Colette Kress now has to manage the commercial business while the company’s founder remains the subject of an extraordinary political and corporate struggle. “The broader institutional positioning suggests why even an outstanding earnings forecast may struggle to generate the kind of rally investors once took for granted.” Also in focus this week is the planned New York debut Thursday of AI giant Anthropic following an initial public offering that is expected to value the firm at as much as US$1.4 trillion. While Anthropic is widely seen as the leader for AI products, Nvidia has been dubbed the “central bank” of the industry for its investments in startups and providing backstops on loans. By the end of the week, traders are hoping to have more certainty about the commercial future of a technology that has been long on hype but short on profitable products. Oil prices continued to fall following reports that the world will swing to a surplus despite the US-Iran war. However, the commodity was supported by ongoing attacks in the Gulf region. Kuwait said today it was countering “hostile drone attacks”, with Washington’s allies on alert following a US strike on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. — AFP

d8c12a562bcb99c7: SHANGHAI: Equities in China and Hong Kong fell as investors continued to offload Chinese AI hardware exporters and AI hyperscalers, amid signs of hardening US tech curbs against China ahead of a meeting between leaders Xi Jinping and Donald Trump.

China's stock benchmark was near 16-month lows as former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's fall from grace following Republicans' defeat in the US midterm election foreshadowed an escalation in Sino-US tensions.

"The downfall of Jensen Huang could have consequences far beyond the AI sector, as tighter financing threatens the investment boom and political tensions reshape US-China relations," Louis-Vincent Gave, founding partner of Gavekal Research, said in a note.
Both China's blue-chip index CSI300 and the Shanghai Composite Index were down roughly 0.4% by the midday break, flirting with the lowest level since mid-2025.
The Trump administration plans to press ahead with efforts to block imports of Chinese data-centre equipment despite pushback from US technology companies.
Reuters reported in August that the Federal Communications Commission was seeking to ban US imports of new models of Chinese optical transceivers over national security concerns.

In a sign the US is tightening exports of advanced chips to China, Nvidia said the company would not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO, and that its outlook assumes no data-centre chip sales to China.
Huang had supported keeping sales open to China.
Chinese optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink, which are heavily reliant on the US market, extended declines. They're down more than 70% from their peaks.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Tech index lost 1.5%, dragged lower by AI model developer MiniMax, as well as tech giants Alibaba and Tencent, whose businesses rely on advanced computing power.
However, China's STAR Chip Index rose 0.5% and an index of China's semiconductor industry gained, on bets that homegrown AI chipmakers will benefit from tighter US chip restrictions.

In other signs of geopolitical tensions, Trump met the leaders of key regional allies India, Japan and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, ahead of a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in Shenzhen.
The Quad expressed "grave concerns" about "economic coercion" in a statement, without naming China.
Meanwhile, US Democratic senator Tammy Baldwin on Tuesday introduced legislation to revoke China's normal trade status and favourable tariff treatment.
In China, gold stocks tumbled nearly 5% on higher expectations of US rate hikes, while defence stocks also fell sharply.

a59da5813cc3318a: NEW DELHI: Amazon said it will invest US$7 billion in India's clean energy projects by 2030 as it steps up efforts to cut the carbon footprint of electricity powering its operations.
The announcement late Tuesday comes as India targets 500GW of clean energy capacity by the end of the decade, a goal the government estimates will require around US$220 billion in investment.
Amazon said the planned spending would help reduce the "carbon intensity of electricity powering its operations" in the world's most populous nation.

The pledge comes on top of US$4 billion in renewable energy investments Amazon has already pledged in India, making it one of the country's leading corporate purchasers of carbon-free electricity, the firm said in a statement on Tuesday.
The e-commerce giant also announced four new wind and solar projects, with a combined capacity of 934MW, under its existing investment programme.
"Our renewable energy investments in India reflect years of sustained effort, planning, and collaboration across the industry," said Kara Hurst, Amazon's chief sustainability officer.
"This additional investment of US$7 billion underlines our long-term commitment, helping bring additional wind and solar capacity online," Hurst said.
The firm did not provide details on how the additional funding would be allocated or which projects it would support.
India has accelerated its shift towards cleaner energy over the past decade, although coal and oil remain central to its energy mix.
More than 54% of the country's installed electricity generation capacity now comes from non-fossil fuel sources, including solar, wind and hydropower.
The expansion of renewable energy is key to India's efforts to meet rising electricity demand while advancing its climate commitments.
For Amazon, the investment also forms part of a broader effort to decarbonise the electricity supply supporting its global operations, including its data centres and other facilities.
e7bb5cbcc3bc3bfa: <!--kg-card-end: html--> A new study from Gallup looked at how young people across the world are making friends, both digitally and in person. The good news is that around 93% of the young people surveyed reported having at least one strong in-person friendship. The weird news is that 33% said they had an AI companion.

Gallup’s study is lengthy and nuanced. It partnered with the Boston Children’s Digital Wellness Lab to conduct the study and used online surveys of more than 16,000 young people from the ages of 15 to 22 in 16 different countries.

A lot of the topline results won’t surprise anyone living in today’s constantly online digital-forward age. Gallup found that respondents felt their in-person friendships were their strongest, that digital friendships complemented rather than replaced in-person ones, and that stronger friendships made people happier no matter how the connection was made. Three things that stood out were how the young respondents talked about AI, loneliness, and doomscrolling.

Young people in the United States, Canada, and UK reported the least interest in AI overall, with only 20% saying they used it once a day or more. Almost 40 percent of young people in Brazil use it daily. Japan and Italy both come in around 35%. “Nearly half of young people in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada have used AI no more than a few times in the past month, including those who have not used it at all,” the researchers wrote.

Most of the respondents (82%) said they’d used AI to look up information, 68% asked it for advice, and 33% used it as a companion. Young people with online-only friends were more likely to use AI for companionship, “although these patterns do not establish whether AI companionship supplements or substitutes for human relationships,” they wrote.

The researchers discovered that people in different countries felt wildly different about their AI buddies. Almost half of Australians with AI friends rated the relationship as “high quality” and only 12% of young people in Poland did. Mostly, though, people thought of their AI friends as mid: “In most countries [...] young people are more likely to give their AI companionship a medium rating than either a high or low rating.”

People who used AI as a friend also reported higher levels of loneliness, the study found. “However, the findings cannot determine whether young people turn to AI because they feel lonely, whether AI companionship influences their social experiences or whether other circumstances help explain these relationships,” the researchers wrote.

The researchers also asked young people what they do online all day and the overwhelming majority (72%) said they spend their time scrolling short form content, mostly TikTok and Instagram. It’s also how they deal with loneliness, with six in 10 young people participating in this study reporting that they often or always scroll through online content when lonely.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> They also said scrolling works to dispel loneliness almost equally as well as hanging out with a friend in real life: “Although scrolling is more commonly used when young people feel lonely, those who use scrolling or in-person time as coping strategies report nearly identical levels of perceived helpfulness.”

Still, people who reported strong in-person friendships said they felt lonely less often, while online friendships have the same effect on loneliness regardless of how participants ranked the quality of those friendships. “No comparable difference appears across levels of online-only friendship quality,” the authors wrote. Having in-person relationships seemed to be what mattered most: “Higher loneliness is also more common among young people who frequently communicate online with strangers or online-only friends than among those who frequently communicate with in-person friends or family members.”

The relationships between loneliness, online friendships, and AI is complex and a person’s material conditions shape how they form friendships more than their access to a chatbot or how they use social media. The researchers’ analysis of young people who said they have no trusted adults in their lives makes that clear.

“Further analysis identifies several characteristics associated with having none of these friendship modes, but one stands out in particular: not having a trusted adult outside the family,” the researchers wrote. “This association remains substantial after accounting for country or residence, gender, age, urbanicity, and parent/ caregiver relationship quality.”

The study’s authors warned about reading too much into these results. “These assessments should be compared cautiously with those for human friendships examined in this report, as young people may have different expectations of what makes an AI companion or human friendship meaningful or supportive,” they wrote. In general, people don’t have the same expectations of a chatbot that they do someone they know in real life.

“The broader message is not that one form of connection is inherently better or worse, but that the quality of young people’s relationships and the wider social context in which they exist matter greatly,” the study concluded.

461a1fe87414da12: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector.  Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper, the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference.  However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text.  For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector resilient to these distribution shifts. Adaptation in action In TTA, instead of freezing the model so it can’t change during deployment, researchers allow that model to adapt itself to incoming data after it has been released. For an AI text detector, these data are new pieces of text uploaded by users.  These data are unlabeled, so the detector developers don’t know which data were written by humans versus AI models. But these new data represent contemporary human and AI writing — exactly what the developers want the model to be able to predict.  With enough examples, the detector learns to identify patterns to determine which data are AI-generated and which are human-generated. The researchers studied TTA by creating datasets to contain a certain amount of AI-generated and human-generated text, but they don’t provide those labels to the model. They also used LLMs to generate some examples that resemble text written by AI to specifically evade a detector.  Then they performed the TTA training process and tested the model on ground-truth data. In experiments designed to mimic the natural shift in human language over time, a detector that used TTA was 85 percent accurate, while traditional methods only achieved 73 percent accuracy. And when it came to writing designed to thwart detection tools, existing methods could only identify about 27 percent, while TTA enabled the model to catch more than 93 percent of disguised text. “TTA has the potential to really help deployed AI-detection models in terms of being able to proactively address this iterative ‘gaming’ behavior by adversarial AI users,” Ren says. Adapting to shifts in human writing behavior is a more difficult TTA problem, since the shifts are slower and occur in more subtle ways, he adds. The researchers caution that TTA may not always be an effective solution as future LLMs produce more natural-sounding language and it becomes harder to find verifiable human text to use for training. “It isn’t entirely clear if this will be a solvable problem,” Raghavan says. “There are some big, open questions about how you should think about science, writing, and art in a world where it is infeasible to tell the difference between human-generated content and AI content.” In the future, the researchers want to explore similar strategic domains where TTA could be useful and build better benchmarking tools to help engineers improve these AI detection models in a dynamic fashion. This project used API credits provided by Pangram to use their AI text detectors.
