a3cb9e0745e497c9: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa. The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region. However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor. Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution. Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait. Our years of research and forthcoming book “Refugees Without Refuge” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies. A corridor for travel, trade and escape Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters. For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents. Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence. Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours. Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls. The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas. Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate. A lifeline for those escaping conflict Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade. The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers. The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti. Members of the Djiboutian coast guard inspect boats seized from ‘delalas’ attempting to transport migrants to Yemen on April 12, 2026. Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait. As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad. A humanitarian corridor Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel. UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño. In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin. Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region. c183c48b2575ee6b: <!--kg-card-end: html--> In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account.

I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents.

A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”

The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful.

“I would hope that, if this goes to court and Meta shows up, a judge would say ‘You know what, this is a system you built, that you put out there and sold to people, it’s a system you believe in.’ I would think your own system [Baby Mia] has a right to be heard in this case,” Thomas said.

Baby Mia didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. Thomas sent me a “Privacy Act Release” from Scott’s office that gave the Senator permission to use Thomas’s info to get him access back to his accounts. Scott’s office put “Baby Mia — AI assistant to Joe Thomas” as a person who should be kept updated on the case.

47a7c5b0482b14c4: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

47ff0aa6ed8c896f: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage.

But when scientists studied satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes around the world since the year 2000, they discovered that lakes “are undergoing a profound shift toward spatial synchrony through time” that “strongly indicates that increasing lake synchrony is a genuine, global-scale phenomenon,“ according to the study.

“Lakes, although covering less than 2 percent of Earth’s surface, play disproportionate roles in regulating global biogeochemical cycles and macroscale ecological dynamics,” said researchers led by Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

“They bury carbon at rates far exceeding those of the oceans, store roughly half as much organic carbon as terrestrial soils, emit greenhouse gases equivalent to ~20 percent of fossil fuel emissions, recycle nutrients that structure regional and global biogeochemical cycles, and sustain exceptional levels of biodiversity. Lakes are also critically important social–ecological systems, providing vital ecosystem services for billions.”

Yet despite the important role they play in supporting life and modulating the climate, lakes are typically managed on local or regional levels. This approach will have to change as lakes approach global synchrony, rendering them more vulnerable to heatwaves, droughts, and the encroachment of urban development, all of which contribute to the phenomenon, according to the study.

“Coincident algal blooms or hypoxia events could trigger parallel lake ecosystem collapses across continents, eroding the regional diversity essential for ecosystem recovery and adaptation,” Zhang’s team said in the study. “In effect, increasing synchrony erodes the spatial asynchrony that once buffered local disturbances, indicating a shift toward geographically widespread ecological responses to shared global pressures.”

Zhang and his colleagues were able to confirm the increase in synchrony across three datasets: satellite-derived chlorophyll levels, water transparency in thousands of lakes, and sedimentary records from 119 lakes spanning the past century. The results suggest that lakes are no longer a varied patchwork of environments, but an increasingly interwoven system that must be addressed on national and global levels.

“The emerging evidence for increasing global lake synchrony calls for a conceptual shift: lake ecosystems can no longer be viewed as isolated systems experiencing local degradation, but should also be recognized as sensitive indicators of increasingly coupled environmental pressures,” the researchers said.
“Our findings support this hypothesis and indicate that the synchronized, planetary-scale behaviors of lakes are an emergent property of the Anthropocene,” the team concluded.
dcc8a79edd081eef: Pavel L Photo and Video/ShutterstockOn August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake. The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning. While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature. Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it. Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres. And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged. Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels. When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change. Leer más: Three things historical literature can teach us about the climate crisis Reading from the future The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work. In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea. The Thwaites glacier, in the eastern Antarctic, is shrinking fast, and is losing significant amounts of ice. NASA/James Yungel, CC BY-SA Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future. An unexpected atlas Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way. In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it? Leer más: The Antarctic ice sheet is melting. And this is bad news for humanity Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change. Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them. eb072ea9f9570323: James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era. Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s. In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged. Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma. Pattinson’s career Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles. From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective. There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig. Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024. Pattinson’s Bond As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity. In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity. I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond. Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity. Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability. Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture. Read more: I write James Bond novels – here’s why Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight will bring a crackling new intensity to 007 In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced. I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim. dc806d9aba93926c: The ongoing security situation has made the country’s healthcare crisis worse
Originally published on Global Voices
Image by Global Voices, created using Canva elements.

Haiti is a country with very few health facilities and a dearth of healthcare workers to meet people’s needs. Public hospitals lack basic medical equipment, demand far exceeds staff capacity, and administrative problems are rife.

Other health centres, usually run by non-profit organisations, help some of the most vulnerable people, while private hospitals are few and far between, given that most Haitians cannot afford to pay for treatment there. Even the wealthy are often forced to go abroad for treatment when faced with critical health issues.

This already dire situation became worse when gangs from the Viv Ansanm criminal coalition began targeting both public and private health facilities, looting many of them, stealing equipment, and even setting fire to some of the properties. Health centres located in gang-controlled areas are often forced to close temporarily because of fights that break out between rival gangs.

Enter the challenge of street medicine vendors, mobile drugstores, and sellers operating from kiosks. Practically everywhere you go — on sidewalks and public markets, inside bus stations and more — you can find hucksters selling medicine out of buckets and bags, or from small stalls. These vendors have no professional medical training; yet they often “prescribe” drugs that have nothing to do with their customers’ health concerns. Sold in questionable conditions on the street, in heat and dust, these “medicines” pose a serious danger to consumers’ lives.

No Haitian government has fought effectively against this issue. Because most people cannot afford private health centres, they self-medicate, taking these drugs without medical advice. In many cases, the drugs are either expired, spoiled, fake, or do not work as promised. While licensed drug stores are operating, they are small in number compared to the many unauthorised vendors that line the streets.

In a YouTube video on the channel Sedney the Reporter with host Sedney Saint-Fleur, Dr Wellington Derameau, a doctor, pharmacist, and researcher who completed several specialised university training programmes in the United States and France, spoke about the problems in Haiti’s pharmaceutical sector.

That public concern over low-quality medicine led him, in collaboration with the University of Colorado and the Faculty of Medicine at the State University of Haiti, to test the quality of pharmaceuticals circulating across Haiti, particularly in the capital, Port-au-Prince. In 2020, they published the first scientific paper, showing the results of tests in which researchers sampled roughly 258 boxes of antibiotics across 28 open-air markets in Port-au-Prince:

Nou te jwenn 6 antimikwobyen (antibiyotik) sou 11 ki pa t gen okenn konfòmite spèktr. Sa vle di, lòske nou fè des analiz poussées, nou wè ke medikaman sa yo nou te ranmase nan lari a yo pa gen anyen pou wè ak medikaman, pa gen prensip aktif.

We found that six out of 11 antibiotic types failed basic spectral compliance testing. Advanced laboratory analysis revealed that these street-bought products contained no active ingredients whatsoever.

Selling drugs without active compounds in this informal market leaves patients without effective treatment and accelerates antimicrobial resistance. Dr Derameau highlighted cases where patients bought “amoxicillin” expecting a functioning antibiotic, but received capsules filled with starch:
Mache paralèl la fragilize mache legal la, se premye konsta pa m pa rapò ak sa, epi li mete an evidans movèz kalite medikaman yo.
The parallel market undercuts the regulated sector, directly contributing to the spread of substandard medicine.

Official statistics from the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP) for the 2025–2026 fiscal year underline the scope of the problem. Across the nation, only 101 pharmaceutical companies, 49 storage drugstores, 49 import agencies, and three local manufacturing labs hold valid licenses, while some geographic departments lack any legal pharmaceutical representation.
This vacuum, Dr Derameau emphasised, feeds a real threat to public health:
Donc le constat est criant par rapport avec la non-réglementation des pharmacies dans le pays, tout sa pral anjandre nou avèk yon cercle vicieux de vente illicite des médicaments.
The lack of pharmacy regulation creates a glaring threat, trapping the country in a vicious cycle of illicit medicine sales.
Compounded by widespread gang violence and insecurity, these unregulated sales leave the population without reliable access to essential healthcare.

Dr Derameau shared a sad anecdote from his time at Hôpital Universitaire La Paix, involving a child suffering from acute glomerulonephritis. Curious why the patient was not improving, he asked the parents to show him the medicines they were administering. Upon checking, he saw that the medicine was inappropriate for the child’s condition and did not match what had been prescribed. If he hadn’t discovered this in time, it could have led to the child’s death, and nobody would have known the cause because of the absence of forensic facilities in the country:

Mwen pa bezwen di'w ki kantite lòt moun ki viktim, chak desè ta sipoze dokimante pou ale gade koz ki alawouz li malerezman, c'est pas le cas, mwen pran egzanp grenn echantiyon sa donc mwen menm mwen veku, men pa bezwen di'w ki kantite lòt moun ki viktim pa rapò avèk movèz medikaman.

I do not need to tell you how many other people are victims; every death is supposed to be documented to look at the root cause, but unfortunately, that is not the case. I take this single example that I personally experienced, but I do not need to tell you how many other people are victims because of bad medicines.

The child’s parents bought the medicine from a street vendor stationed directly in front of the public hospital, where it is common to find small kiosks and mobile vendors offering different types of medication, and using loudspeakers to advertise all kinds of drugs for various illnesses.

The lion’s share of medication being sold on the Haitian market, Dr Derameau said, comes from India and the Dominican Republic (DR). However, there are also many products with no listed origin at all, which he considers an anomaly. Authorised pharmaceutical laboratories respect quality standards, he explained, as do legitimate importation agencies. The vulnerable area, however, is the border, which serves as the main entry point for contraband.

Although quality control and verification institutions exist alongside the national laboratory as public bodies responsible for regulating the importation, manufacturing, and sale of medicines, this does not stop all kinds of drugs from circulating freely on the market without any real oversight.

Even as he stressed that not all medicines imported from the Dominican Republic are sub-standard, Haiti is flooded with many low-quality drugs, especially when it comes to medications that are in high demand. From his work experience at the Justinien University Hospital in Cap-Haïtien, Dr Derameau also discovered that many of these medicines are not registered with the Ministry of Public Health:
Yo soti nan lòt sirkwit la atravè les fwontyè yo. Gen des laboratwa an Repiblik Dominikèn k ap ponpe nou des medikaman ki pwòp pou Ayiti.
They enter through the other channel across the borders. There are laboratories in the Dominican Republic pumping out medicines made specifically for Haiti.

Noting that generic medicines manufactured by local pharmaceutical laboratories — which number three in total — are very good and respect quality standards, he also posited that there is an industry manufacturing fake medicines within Haiti itself, and called on the state to investigate.

The security crisis is not helping matters. Roads leading to the Great North and Great South — as well as parts of Port-au-Prince — are controlled by various gangs, creating a major obstacle for the free movement of medicine, as well as access to health centres and other distribution points. He highlighted the sabotage and looting that many pharmacies suffered in downtown Port-au-Prince:

Chaîne d'approvisionnement an, insécurité a gen anpil enpak sou li, donk li kraze disponibilité médicaments yo, donc patient vin soufri, marché noir fèt ak médicaments sa yo. Imajine'w tout pharmacie ki te anba lavil la ke bandi yo kase (piye). Gen lòt fenomèn, se machann kap vann nan bus yo kap chanje dat expiration médicaments yo epi y ap vann yo. Donc insécurité a impacté qualité de vie moun yo, insécurité a impacté qualité soins yo, insécurité a impacté protocole thérapeutique yo.

The security crisis heavily impacts the supply chain, thereby destroying medicine availability, causing patients to suffer, and creating a black market for these drugs. Imagine all the pharmacies downtown that bandits looted. There is another phenomenon where vendors selling on buses change the expiration dates on medicines and sell them. So insecurity impacts people’s quality of life, insecurity impacts the quality of care, and insecurity impacts therapeutic protocols.

The challenges around transporting medicines also drive black-market demand and further increase border contraband. Yet Dr Derameau says he is optimistic that if the state shows real political will and enforces strict regulations, it can end these practices.
Written by Jude Pierre Louis
3a3d3d52559d0da4: Lawyers for the Department of Justice are using the AI writing detection service Pangram to argue that opposing attorneys are using AI to write legal arguments, and in one case told the court that opposing counsel was doing “defense by ChatGPT,” and writing “AI slop” filings, according to court filings reviewed by 404 Media.

Over the last few years, we have documented many attorneys getting caught by judges using AI after citing hallucinated cases that do not exist. The filings in this court case over the past month show attorneys, including those working for the government, are trying to catch each other using AI, then are citing their opponents’ AI use in their arguments to the court.

“This case has turned into defense by ChatGPT,” government attorneys wrote in the case, which centers around a high-profile voter fraud case. “Motions practice in this case is the equivalent of writing responses to documents generated by a robot that is attempting to practice law. It cannot be that the local rules envisioned that it was acceptable for defense to use what the kids would call ‘AI slop’ to create multiple frivolous motions that waste judicial resources and fail to serve the cause of justice.”

The defendant is Khalwinder Bhengura, an Indian man who entered the United States on an immigrant visa in 2022 and illegally — and apparently accidentally, according to his lawyers — registered to vote in Texas in 2024 after falsely stating that he was an American citizen on his application for a driver’s license. Bhengura was arrested in September on charges of lying about his citizenship status, illegally registering to vote, and illegally voting in the 2024 election, and was found guilty in October on two of the three counts. His family and lawyers have argued that the whole thing is a misunderstanding, and that Bhengura, who is 70 years old and does not speak English well, did not know he was committing a crime and did not understand what he was doing.

Bhengura has been in prison for months and is set to be deported. He is now not only being held up as an example by the Trump administration of voter fraud but is also now caught in the middle of an AI lawyering dispute.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Three hours and 15 minutes into the 4 hour long documentary Musk, a video game avatar of the titular billionaire picks up a chainsaw off the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. Shot like a first-person shooter, the audience watches as Musk wields the chainsaw to destroy various government buildings. Walking through a farm, Musk aims the chainsaw at grain silos labeled ‘USDA’ and lightning arcs from its spinning blades. The silo explodes and cows moo in distress.

In my experience, the purpose of a video game chainsaw is to viscerally rend through objects. I have never seen one shoot lightning. It’s a small detail that speaks to my overall problem with Alex Gibney’s Musk: it’s cringe.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> Elon Musk is one of the most powerful men alive on the planet and Gibney’s Musk does a decent job of giving the overall arc of the man’s many faults. The director takes us from Zip2 to DOGE while highlighting the billionaire’s pathology, and it hits more than it misses.

Musk is a good overview of the general arc of Elon Musk, the man. But there have been other Elon Musk documentaries told in much the same way (we made one at VICE several years ago, that is similar in tone and vibe). And so, at a laborious four hours long, it’s not clear who Musk is for, and the weird video game interstitials and ghoulish AI avatar of Musk himself are genuinely distracting. Musk would not talk to Gibney so the director generated an AI avatar of the billionaire to act as a stand-in. Throughout Musk, this hyperreal grotesque lends color commentary as if the billionaire is actually in the room.

The director cites Musk’s oft-stated belief that we’re living in a simulation as a justification for the AI Musk. “He believed it likely that an artificial intelligence of the future had exfiltrated all knowledge and life experiences from planet Earth and was now running an ancestor simulation in which our past lives had become the training data for a kind of sim world,” Gibney says as the AI musk coalesces before the audience. “In honor of that idea, we decided to edit together recordings of his actual words to create a simulated interview at the heart of a kind of documentary video game.

I understand what Musk is going for here, and it’s funny to watch Musk’s likeness and spirit rendered through the lens of AI and video games. But, on the whole, the AI Elon doesn’t work. Its head is too big, its features are exaggerated, and it sits in a stereotypical gamer chair while bathed in the kind of blue and red lighting popular on Twitch streams ten years ago. The things the bot says aren’t fabricated, they’re direct quotes from the man himself, though some are lightly edited.
In every instance, the quotes are more interesting and more informative when shown in their actual context, in the video interviews the real Musk gave.
“I lost my son, essentially. They call it dead naming because, uh, your son is dead. So my son is dead. Killed by the woke mind virus,” AI Elon says in the film.

This was part of an interview with Jordan Peterson for The Daily Wire. Learning that enriches the quote. There’s crosstalk with Peterson. You see Musk’s real face when he talks about Vivian. It is a real video interview that you can actually watch. There is no need to use an AI avatar to do this.

In another clip the AI Elon explains the Twitter Files. “On Twitter, there was a lot of censorship. We sort of uncovered a lot of that with the Twitter Files,” it says. “Free speech is meaningless unless you allow people you don’t like to say things you don’t like.” The real clip comes from a Real Time With Bill Maher interview.

There’s a lot of this in the film. “What is the most entertaining outcome for the election? That’s probably what’s going to happen,” the Musk bot grins evilly while paraphrasing a Musk catchphrase. Musk talking to Kara Swisher, Musk at a Vanity Fair conference, Musk delivering missives at CPAC, and Musk speaking to Joe Rogan are all condensed into an AI approximation of the real person. In every instance, the original quote in its context is more powerful and more illuminating about its subject.

And then there’s the video game sequences. Musk uses Elon’s obsession with video games as an extended visual metaphor throughout. Under a pink filter that looks like it’s designed to capitalize on the release of Grand Theft Auto VI, Musk picks different classes — shifting from gamer to founder to Kublai Khan. He drives a sports car along a digital track while Tesla’s stock pieces rises like a video game score, and uses Iron Man-style gloves to vaporize Twitter employees.

If the man believes we’re living in a video game then this is what it might look like. His DOGE -fueled chainsaw rampage across DC ends with him dropping a nuke on the National Nuclear Safety Administration and his inauguration Nazi salute turned into a pixel-art version score screen.

Again, this is a four-hour long documentary. It has an intermission, even when you stream it. The video game sequences and AI Elon feel like a baby boomer grasping the aesthetics of a younger generation and misusing them. It’s Steve Buscemi holding a skateboard in the hallway of a high school asking how his fellow kids are doing. It detracts from the overall message here, which is that Musk is a destructive force in our businesses and politics.

After publication, Musk’s public relations team reached out to 404 Media to say, “The Musk avatar was made with CGI and was hand-designed, AI was only used to sync the sound to the image they created," a representative from Falco Ink told 404 Media.

In multiple interviews about Musk, Gibney himself calls the avatar AI. “You need to embrace the air of unreality in order to bring a sense of reality to bear. You have to explore the tools of deception and manipulation to get out the other side. That’s why we came up with the AI avatar of Elon Musk,” Gibney told the International Documentary Association.

“The AI elements that we used were really to get the sync, and even that was interesting [...] we were using an AI artist at Makemake and very much using the tools to try to refine stuff. But it wasn’t like generative AI where you press a button and suddenly this slop appears,” Gibney told Edward Niedermeyer in an interview. “We gave it a lot of consideration.”
Update: This piece has been updated with a statement from Musk’s public relations team and more context from comments Gibney has made.

82a0f3f376656399: Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all.

The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user's knowledge.

Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent's reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.”

70974fc45b43c06a: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — Speculation over Anthropic’s stock market valuation has highlighted one of the riskiest bets in finance: trying to put a price on the future of artificial intelligence.
A few days before its initial public offering, the maker of the AI agent Claude said it was aiming for a market capitalisation of up to US$1.4 trillion (RM5.73 trillion).
That figure would put the young company among the largest stock market debuts on record, though it falls short of the US$2 trillion (RM8.18 trillion) some estimates had floated until a few weeks ago.
Since then, concern about AI development and profits has swept the market.
OpenAI, a rival which plans to go public in 2027, is valued at US$1.025 trillion (RM4.19 trillion) on the private market, according to US media reports.
There are two main ways to value a company, said Michelle Lowry, a finance professor at Drexel University.
The first is to estimate how much cash the company will bring in over the coming years.
Money expected far in the future counts for less than money today, especially when it is uncertain, so those future amounts are reduced to work out what the company is worth now.
The second compares the company with similar listed firms.
If those firms are valued at, say, five times their annual revenue, the same ratio is applied to the company being valued.
Both methods are well established, but “in the case of Anthropic, both of these approaches are quite difficult,” Lowry told AFP.
Like most AI companies, Anthropic is still burning through cash and has not found a path to profitability, which makes its future cash flows hard to forecast.
It also has few listed peers.
The closest is SpaceX, which made a record debut on Wall Street in June with a valuation of US$1.77 trillion (RM7.24 trillion).
But that comparison is imperfect, since the Elon Musk-led company combines a social network, space operations and an AI lab.
SpaceX also rides on Musk’s star power among retail investors.
‘Back and forth’
So how was the US$1.4 trillion (RM5.73 trillion) figure set?
“There’s some back and forth process” between companies seeking to go public and institutional investors, said Minmo Gahng, an assistant professor of finance at Cornell University.
Investment banks act as intermediaries between the two sides, he said, in a process that can be very time-consuming.
A company’s valuation is its share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding.
A company going public wants that price as high as possible, since it determines how much money it raises.
But it also has to leave enough room to attract buyers, since weak demand would drag down the stock.
Investors, for their part, want to be sure they can later sell their stakes at a profit – and are hoping for a “pop,” or sharp rise in the share price, on the first day of trading.
Speaking Friday with JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei cited a company motto when discussing the IPO: “underpromise and overdeliver.”
He also said the company was going public mainly because it needs funding.
Anthropic is set to raise a total of US$90 billion (RM368.1 billion) through the offering, money it plans to use to develop cutting-edge AI.
‘No guarantee’

Jay Ritter, an IPO specialist at the University of Florida, said investors accept such valuations because a handful of companies, such as Amazon, Alphabet and Nvidia, have shown “you can earn profits of US$100 billion (RM409 billion) a year or more without competition eroding those profits.”
But there is “no guarantee” that Anthropic will do the same, he warned.
“It could be the case that 10 years from now, Anthropic will have been left in the dust where nobody is using frontier large language models because open source models are good enough and cheap.”

Anthropic’s growth has already shown signs of slowing and 90 pages of its IPO prospectus are devoted to risks facing the future of the company – and even of humanity – depending on the direction AI takes. — AFP

4111a81bc2e14429: The court ruled that soldiers who committed criminal offenses should be tried by civilian courts
Originally published on Global Voices
Constitutional Court of Indonesia in Jakarta. Photo by Christophe95. Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that the 1997 Military Justice Law would be invalid unless amended within two years. The decision was hailed by human rights groups because it means soldiers who commit crimes can be tried in civilian courts.

Article 9 of the Military Justice Law requires active-duty personnel of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to be held accountable exclusively under the military justice system, even when they commit ordinary criminal offenses and human rights violations.
The law was a legacy of the New Order era when the country was under the strongman rule of Suharto, who relied on the military establishment to hold power from 1966 until his resignation in 1998.

The October 15 court ruling was celebrated by human rights groups that have long advocated for the overhaul of the law. They have documented how military courts have failed to investigate and prosecute grave abuses committed by soldiers. They have also expressed concern that military judges are active-duty soldiers, and that judicial investigations and prosecutions often take place within the military chain of command and behind closed doors, with no public oversight.

One of the petitioners asking officials to revoke the law was Eva Meliani Pasaribu, the daughter of Tribrata TV journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu, who was killed in June 2024 after reporting about a gambling operation allegedly involving a high-level military official. The military conducted a closed-door investigation and dismissed the allegation for lack of evidence.
Ibnu Syamsu Hidayat, the legal counsel for the petition, addressed the court during the hearing and explained how the law erodes civilian supremacy within a democratic system of governance.

“The dominance of military court jurisdiction over the general judiciary is considered inconsistent with the principles of a constitutional democracy, which mandates that civilian authority must take precedence over military power.”
Hidayat added that the law’s broad provisions have been interpreted to include other criminal offenses committed by soldiers.

“It allows them not only to try military personnel or those equated with them for military crimes and disciplinary violations, but also to adjudicate other criminal cases such as corruption, traffic offenses, domestic violence, narcotics, psychotropics, and child protection cases.”

During the hearing, numerous high-level military officers spoke up in defense of the law. The director general of Defense Forces at the Ministry of Defense, Marshal H. Haris Haryanto, argued that the actions of soldiers, including criminal violations, “can also affect the solidarity and readiness of the military institution.” He added, “Military courts are designed to understand these characteristics so they can deliver decisions that satisfy a sense of justice while also taking into account the interests of national defense.”

The commander of the National Armed Forces, General Agus Subiyanto, said the petition questioning the effectiveness, independence, and accountability of the military justice system “is not based on a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of military law.”

He emphasized that military judges have the independence of judicial power guaranteed by the constitution and are under the technical judicial supervision of the Supreme Court, adding, “In a military organization, discipline is the primary foundation of national strength. Therefore, the commander’s authority to ensure due process for his subordinates is an inherent legal obligation to maintain operational readiness and the institution’s honor.”

Legal experts who participated in the hearing disagreed, arguing that the law needs reform in order to comply with current human rights standards. Al Araf told the court that the law was drafted under the framework of an “authoritarian political regime” that ignored the principles of rule of law.

“During the New Order era, the legal products enacted in the form of statutes tended to be repressive and merely served as instruments of control for those in power,” he said. “The state enacted laws not within the framework of the rule of law, but solely to fulfill the needs of the rule by law.”
Zainal Arifin Mochtar, another legal expert at the hearing, said the law has to be updated to conform with democratic principles.

“Many issues have emerged, ranging from dual jurisdictions, a lack of synchronization with the spirit of reform, the absence of detailed regulations regarding connectivity, to the issue of independence and accountability of military justice, which is often discussed as a form of legal exceptionalism,” he said.

The move has been widely celebrated by human rights defenders. The Indonesian human rights group KontraS welcomed the court decision, noting that one of its employees has been subjected to an acid attack perpetrated by a group of soldiers. Under the new ruling, soldiers could be tried in public courts in such cases.

“This ruling closes a legal loophole that has long been perceived as protecting individual soldiers from accountable law enforcement, while also marking a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and fulfilling the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia,” read their statement.
The reform is the result of decades of work and activism, as explained by Human Rights Watch (HRW).

“Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” read their statement. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”
Free Press Unlimited said the court ruling is a victory against impunity.

“The Constitutional Court’s eagerly awaited ruling is a true victory for justice and a critical step for Indonesia in its fight against impunity,” read their statement on the ruling. “We urge lawmakers to act promptly and adhere to this landmark ruling as soon as possible. Only then can Indonesia finally turn a corner and ensure that cases involving military personnel will be dealt with by civilian courts, as it should be.”

Both Indonesian and international civil society groups are urging lawmakers to start the reform process by consulting the public and various stakeholders. Activists argue that public vigilance has to be sustained, especially since Indonesia’s current president, Prabowo Subianto, is a former general dismissed from the military for committing human rights violations. Since coming to power in 2024, he has expanded the military’s role in civilian governance.
Written by Mong Palatino
